articles.abstract: Existing literature has largely overlooked how listeners process intonation in synthesised speech and whether music training can modulate performance. Previous research has linked music training to enhanced phrase-final intonation perception and a possible but disputed advantage for processing noise-embedded speech. This study compared musicians and non-musicians in their ability to distinguish statements from declarative questions in low-quality synthesised speech. Stimuli were generated using eSpeak, an open-source speech synthesiser, with half of the stimuli presented in reverse word order. In total, 124 participants (59 musicians and 65 non-musicians) took part. A mixed-effects logistic regression model showed that statements were identified significantly more accurately than declarative questions. Normal word order was also associated with better intonation discrimination relative to reverse word order. Furthermore, musicians outperformed non-musicians, identifying synthesised declarative questions and statements with higher accuracy. Findings are discussed in light of previous research into natural intonation, synthesised speech, and music training.

articles.title: Depressive Symptom Trajectories Around the Retirement Transition Across Countries and Historical Periods
articles.authors: Yufei Zhang; Zhihao Ma
articles.abstract: As global aging accelerates, retirement has become a critical transition in older adults’ lives, with profound implications for mental health. Depression trajectories around retirement are inconsistent, with some studies suggesting worsening symptoms and others indicating improvement. Using HRS (United States, 1994–2020), SHARE (Europe and Israel, 2004–2022), CHARLS (China, 2011–2020), and KLoSA (South Korea, 2006–2020), this study examined depressive symptom trajectories around retirement. We emphasized three key components of the retirement transition: retirement age, pre-retirement phase, and post-retirement phase. Using multilevel models, we estimated changes in depressive symptoms around retirement transition, accounting for cross-national and historical differences. Results showed that depressive symptom trajectories varied across datasets and historical periods, but average changes were generally modest. HRS showed pre-retirement increases, an immediate rise at retirement, and post-retirement decline. SHARE showed mainly a small immediate decrease, CHARLS showed a steady increase across the retirement transition, and KLoSA showed an immediate increase followed by post-retirement decline. Period-specific analyses showed further variation, although many trajectories remained close to stable; in CHARLS, later retirement periods showed steeper post-retirement increases. The findings show that retirement-related changes in depressive symptoms are often modest at the group level, while small departures from stability may vary by temporal phase and historical context.

articles.title: Conversing with a disagreeing LLM improves people’s inaccurate predictions
articles.authors: Emir Efendic; Philippe van de Calseyde
articles.abstract: Accurately predicting the outcome of future events improves decisions in domains ranging from health to finance, yet prediction errors are common. One reliable way to improve accuracy is to engage with disagreeing views through dialogue, which can reveal weak assumptions and facilitate belief revision. However, people often avoid disagreeing exchanges because they are socially and emotionally costly or inconvenient to seek out. Here, we examine whether a disagreeing large language model (LLM) can provide the benefits of disagreement while sidestepping these interpersonal barriers. Across two experiments (total N = 807 adults making 4,564 predictions; Experiment 2 was incentivized and preregistered), participants: i) predicted the likelihood of various events, ii) discussed each prediction with an LLM by articulating their reasoning, and iii) submitted final predictions. Crucially, we manipulated the LLM’s stance during these discussions: it responded either supportively (agreeing) or critically (disagreeing) to participants’ reasoning. The results showed that, when initial predictions were erroneous, conversing with a disagreeing LLM produced more accurate final predictions than conversing with a supportive one. This advantage was primarily driven by directionally correct revisions, with participants shifting their final predictions more often toward the realized outcome. However, interacting with an LLM was not uniformly beneficial as it decreased accuracy when initial predictions were already accurate. These findings underscore the value of designing LLMs that challenge rather than affirm users’ views and opinions, while highlighting the importance of tailoring their responses to the expected accuracy of initial predictions.

articles.title: Social Origins of the Self: Mutual Gaze at 12 Months Predicts Self-Recognition and Fronto-Temporoparietal Connectivity at 18 Months
articles.authors: Emanuela Yeung; Helena-Céline Stevelt; Dimitris Askitis; Helle Lukowski Duplessy; Victoria Southgate
articles.abstract: A central question in developmental science concerns how a reflective, conceptual self emerges. Theoretical accounts propose that infants' early experiences as the object of caregiver attention — particularly through mutual gaze — scaffold the development of objective self-awareness, possibly via maturation of fronto-temporoparietal networks implicated in self-referential processing. The present longitudinal study examined associations among early mutual gaze experience, fronto-temporoparietal functional connectivity, and mirror self-recognition during the second year of life. Mother–infant dyads (N = 107) participated in a 10-min free-play interaction at 12 months, from which mother-to-infant, infant-to-mother, and mutual gaze durations were micro-coded. Task-free functional connectivity within a fronto-temporoparietal network (FTPN) was assessed at 12 and 18 months using fNIRS, and mirror self-recognition was tested at 18 months as an index of self-awareness. Bayesian analyses revealed moderate evidence that infants who experienced more mutual gaze with their mothers at 12 months were more likely to be classified as mirror recognisers at 18 months. Mutual gaze at 12 months also predicted left-hemisphere and bilateral FTPN connectivity at 18 months. We did not replicate previously reported group differences in FTPN connectivity between mirror recognisers and non-recognisers. Together, these findings provide longitudinal evidence that early experience as the object of caregiver attention is associated with the emergence of self-awareness and the development of brain networks implicated in self-referential processing. This supports theoretical accounts situating the origins of objective self-awareness in early dyadic social experience.

articles.title: A Brief Measure of Negative Mind-Wandering: Validation and Incremental Prediction of Depressive Symptoms and Anxiety
articles.authors: Carl-Richard Villanger Løberg; Stefan Koelsch
articles.abstract: Negative self-generated thought is a central feature of both mind-wandering and rumination and plays a key role in depression and anxiety. Brief measures specifically designed to assess negative mind-wandering and suited for repeated assessment are scarce. We developed the Negative Mind-Wandering Inventory (NMWI), a 6-item self-report measure assessing intrusive, repetitive, negatively valenced self-generated thought that is difficult to control and emotionally distressing. In a sample of 77 adults assessed weekly over four weeks, we evaluated internal consistency, factor structure, convergent validity with established rumination measures, and criterion and incremental validity with depressive symptoms and anxiety. The NMWI showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = .89; ωt = .91) and a predominantly unidimensional factor structure. NMWI scores correlated moderately to strongly with established rumination measures and explained additional variance in depressive symptoms and trait anxiety beyond these measures, with medium to large incremental effects. Repeated-measures correlations indicated that within-person fluctuations in NMWI covaried with weekly changes in depressive symptoms and trait anxiety. These findings support the NMWI as a brief, reliable measure with incremental validity for repeated assessment of negative self-generated thought.

articles.title: Affective Reactivity to Social Media Use and Upward Social Comparisons in the Development of Young Adolescents’ Depressive Symptoms
articles.authors: Andrea Irmer (geb. Schmidt); Florian Schmiedek
articles.abstract: Youths differ substantially in how they emotionally respond to daily experiences. Repeated episodes of heightened negative affect in daily life may accumulate over time and increase vulnerability for developing depressive disorders. This study examined whether individual differences in negative affective reactivity to daily experiences (i.e., social media use and upward social comparisons) predict changes in depressive symptoms over time. Using a 14-day diary design with 200 young adolescents (103 female; ages 10–14), we assessed daily social media use, daily upward social comparisons, daily negative affect, and depressive symptoms at pre- and posttest. We employed multilevel structural equation modeling, estimating the within-person coupling between daily social media use (Model 1) or daily upward social comparisons (Model 2) and negative affect and tested whether between-person differences in the strength of this coupling predicted average negative affect and depressive symptom change. Findings revealed that a stronger within-person coupling between upward social comparisons and negative affect, but not between social media use and negative affect, was associated with an increase in depressive symptoms via elevated negative affect across the study. These results highlight the importance of capturing dynamic affective responses to daily comparison experiences when assessing psychological risk in early adolescence.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Activating Social Resources in Psychotherapy-Seeking Individuals: Protocol for a Micro-Randomized Trial Examining the Effectiveness and Timing of a Social Support Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention
articles.authors: Timon Elmer; Nadja Peeters; Markus Wolf; Urte Scholz
articles.abstract:
Background: Depressive symptoms and other mental health issues are highly prevalent worldwide, yet
many healthcare systems struggle to meet the resulting prevention and treatment demands. This disparity
often results in long delays before psychotherapy begins and symptoms may deteriorate during the
searching and waiting period. Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) offer a scalable, digital solution by
providing personalized support during such critical periods. While most existing JITAIs focus on individual-
level exercises (e.g., mindfulness meditations), the mobilization of social resources remains understudied
despite being a well-established protective health factor.
Building on a previous feasibility study, this protocol evaluates a JITAI which was developed based on
existing theory and through a participatory approach. The intervention aims to foster social support
processes for adults with elevated depressive symptoms who are seeking outpatient psychotherapy.
Specifically, the JITAI is designed to increase perceived social support resources and self-care activities
while aiding the social support-seeking process at critical points in daily life, as identified via Ecological
Momentary Assessments (EMAs).
The first objective is to evaluate the JITAI's effectiveness in reducing daily levels of depressive symptoms
and increasing received social support, as primary outcomes. Secondary outcomes are loneliness and
perceived social support. The second objective is to compare the relative efficacy of three JITAI triggering
strategies (i.e., decision rules) to identify the most effective timing for intervention delivery.

Methods: This 21-day micro-randomized trial targets a sample size of 120 psychotherapy-seeking
individuals experiencing elevated depressive symptoms. Participants are randomized on a daily level into
four equally weighted triggering conditions: (1) vulnerability-triggered, (2) vulnerability and receptivity-
triggered, (3) support-need-triggered, and (4) no-intervention control. JITAI triggering data are collected via
five daily EMAs and outcomes are assessed every evening. If triggered, the JITAI is presented directly after
the EMA assessments.

Discussion: If effective, this JITAI provides a low-threshold, personalized digital support to increase the
activation of social resources during the time before formal therapy. By additionally comparing triggering
strategies, this study addresses a critical empirical gap regarding when is “just-in-time” for interventions.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT07471529. Registered on 02.03.2026.

articles.title: Through Their Eyes: Neural and Behavioral Evidence for Enhanced Immersion via  Point-of-View Editing
articles.authors: Moran Ovadia; Shiri Davidovitch; Romi Sion; Naama Shoham; Nimrod Keren; Sergei Freedman; Cynthia Cabanas; Dov Rubinstein; Mark Allen Thornton; Jonathan Frome
articles.abstract: Point-of-view (POV) editing–the juxtaposition of a character’s gaze with the object of that gaze–is presumed to function as a unique empathic device that dissolves spectator-character boundaries; however, direct empirical evidence remains scarce. This study provides the first systematic fMRI and behavioral investigation into whether POV editing facilitates shared attention and intentionality. Thirty-nine adults viewed eight original narrative movies containing POV sequences or closely matched control conditions. POV sequences increased fixation durations on characters’ faces and enhanced subsequent recognition of gazed-at content. Neurally, POV editing elicited stronger responses in regions implicated in mentalizing and increased shared, item-specific activation patterns across viewers within areas associated with perspective-taking and goal-directed control. Multivariate decoding further revealed that a character’s gaze induced more robust neural signatures of character identity on subsequent target elements. Together, these findings support a functional role for POV editing in promoting joint attention and shared intentionality during narrative comprehension.

articles.title: What Pilot Studies Can (and Cannot) Do for Validity in Psychological Research
articles.authors: Yashvin Seetahul; Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; Caroline Zygar-Hoffmann; Lukas Wallrich; Priya Silverstein; Bjørn Sætrevik; Ilse L. Pit; Hannah Loenneker; Neele Henriette Heiser; Isaac J Handley-Miner
articles.abstract: Recent debates about psychology’s credibility have renewed attention to validity threats. We argue that pilot studies can function as methodological due diligence by improving early decisions about design, measurement, manipulation, sampling, and analysis prior to a main study. We examine four types of validity: construct, internal, external, and statistical-conclusion validity. Across these domains, we show how piloting can help researchers assess whether materials and procedures function as intended, identify potential validity threats, and provide key design parameters for planning and model choice. However, we also caution that piloting can harm validity when treated as a consequence-free space in which design or analytic choices are made without disclosing the pilot evidence behind them, or when small, noisy pilots are used to justify overconfident inferences. We therefore argue that when pilots are used to justify substantive design or analytic choices, they should be treated as part of the evidential record and reported transparently. Greater transparency would enable readers to evaluate how pilot evidence shaped the final design of a study and, consequently, better assess the validity of its findings.

articles.title: Inconsistent evidence on lay worker-delivered psychosocial interventions for people who use illicit drugs outside healthcare settings: a systematic review
articles.authors: Trần Thị Hải My; Nguyen Thu Trang; Linda Lux; Nguyen Bich Diep; Jamie Conklin; Ruth Verhey; William C. Miller; Vivian Go; Le Minh Giang; Bradley Gaynes
articles.abstract:
Background. People who use illicit drugs often avoid formal healthcare due to stigma and legal concerns. Lay worker-delivered interventions outside clinical settings offer an accessible alternative. This review evaluated the effectiveness of such interventions on substance use, mental health, and quality of life and explored the patterns across intervention characteristics, target populations and effectiveness. 
Method. We included original studies with trial and pre-post designs. We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, Embase, APA PsycINFO, trial registries and conducted citation searches. Screening, data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. Findings were synthesized using a narrative approach. 
Results. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria: eight targeting people who use drugs in general, two focusing on women, two on men who have sex with men and one on chronic pain patients. Outcomes were synthesised based on the eight studies with low or moderate risk of bias (six randomised controlled trials and two pre-post studies). Across studies, substance use and mental health outcomes improved over time. However, evidence on the additional benefits of lay worker-delivered components was limited, with three trials reporting favourable effects, and three trials reporting no significant differences. Trials with positive findings primarily focused on harm reduction and employed brief, structured interventions; however, the small number of studies limits firm conclusions. 
Conclusion. Lay worker-delivered psychosocial interventions outside healthcare settings may offer a promising and accessible approach for people who use illicit drugs. However, current evidence does not demonstrate consistent additional benefits compared to established interventions, and no clear patterns in effectiveness were identified across populations or intervention characteristics. These findings highlight the need for adequately powered trials incorporating strategies to improve retention and adherence, and implementation-focused research to evaluate the delivery of evidence-based interventions by lay workers.

articles.title: Computational modeling of fixation durations reveals that global inhibition is necessary to explain individual differences in gaze behavior during reading
articles.authors: Daniel Schad; Sarah Risse; Ralf Engbert; Reinhold Kliegl
articles.abstract: Advances in psychological science draw on experimental effects and associated individual differences. Increasingly, advances depend on multivariate statistics and computational modeling of these effects. Here, we examined correlation parameters that were estimated in linear mixed models fitted to eye-movement data from 275 readers as well as to 300 simulations from the SWIFT model of eye-movement control, implementing a narrowing of the attentional span and global inhibition when difficult (i.e., low-frequency) words are fixated. As hypothesized, the model dynamics reproduced a pattern of negative correlations between the fixated word frequency and its two neighbors’ frequencies as well as a positive correlation between the two neighbors found for human readers. Moreover, in simulations with model “lesions”, disabling the zoom lens overpredicted the correlation pattern whereas disabling global inhibition led to a qualitative incompatibility. Integrating experimental, differential, and computational psychology showed global inhibition is needed to explain individual differences in reading.

articles.title: Acoustic and social bonding differences between Japanese singing and conversation: A Registered Report replicating Ozaki et al. (2024)
articles.authors: Gakuto Chiba; Yuto Ozaki; Shinya Fujii; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Understanding cross-cultural differences between singing and speech is a central goal of the Many Voices project (Savage et al. 2025a). As part of this effort, the present study examined Japanese participants (n=10 for confirmatory acoustic analysis; 15 for exploratory behavioural analysis) singing the traditional folk song Tokyo Ondo or having a conversation about favourite foods. Confirmatory analyses replicated previously reported tendencies (Ozaki et al., 2024): singing was higher in pitch, slower in temporal rate, and used more stable pitches than spoken conversation. Temporal rate showed a large effect (Cohen’s d = 1.6), while pitch height (d = 0.55) and pitch stability (d = 0.39) showed medium effect sizes. Exploratory analyses of relationships between acoustic features and social variables suggested that singing increased participants’ self-reported sense of social bonding, and individuals reporting higher perceived synchrony tended to show greater singing–speech differences. This study provides culturally grounded data of Japanese conversation and traditional singing for cross-cultural vocal research and underscores the importance of including traditional repertoires in studies of acoustic variation. The Many Voices project will continue collecting data from up to 24 additional languages and regions, with a subsequent meta-analysis assessing cross-linguistic consistency in singing–speech differences.

articles.title: Comparing Compensatory and Noncompensatory MIRT Models Using Large-Scale Item Response Data
articles.authors: Yiqing Liu; Lijin Zhang; Benjamin Domingue
articles.abstract: A central choice in multidimensional item response theory (MIRT) concerns how multiple latent skills combine to produce success: compensatory models allow trade-offs across dimensions, whereas fully noncompensatory models impose a conjunctive constraint in which limited proficiency on any required dimension can constrain success. Despite longstanding conceptual interest, there is limited evidence on how these skill-combination assumptions affect out-of-sample predictive performance across large-scale assessments. Using the Item Response Warehouse (IRW) and a common missing-responses cross-validation framework, we compare a unidimensional 2PL baseline (1D-2PL) with compensatory and fully noncompensatory two-dimensional 2PL specifications (C2PLM and FNC2PLM) and summarize predictive differences with the InterModel Vigorish (IMV), a portable metric for binary outcomes. A simulation motivates conservative scale thresholds for stable predictive comparisons, after which we conduct empirical analyses across multiple large-scale dichotomous assessments. Across datasets, the compensatory specification yields small (mean IMV = 0.00154) but consistently positive predictive improvements over the unidimensional baseline, whereas the fully noncompensatory specification rarely improves prediction and is seldom preferred over the compensatory alternative (mean IMV = -0.00475). Item-level analyses further reveal within-test heterogeneity, suggesting that conjunctive structure tends to be localized to subsets of items rather than test-wide. These results provide an empirical base-rate reference for comparing skill-combination assumptions under missing-responses prediction and motivate follow-up work that expands to additional assessment programs, relaxes inclusion thresholds to increase dataset diversity, and evaluates alternative prediction targets.

articles.title: Leveraging Norm-Based Ratings to Assess Dimensions of Early Life Adversity: Links to Emotion Regulation and Psychopathology
articles.authors: Mark S. Chen; Alexis Brieant; Leila Adames; Ante Dany; Dylan G. Gee
articles.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of early life adversity (ELA) posit distinct developmental consequences of threat, deprivation, uncontrollability, and unpredictability. Existing approaches force each event into a single dimension or rely on self-ratings that may conflate exposure with subjective appraisal.
Objective: We evaluated norm-based dimensional ratings as an alternative and examined their associations with emotion regulation and psychopathology.
Participants and Setting: A Prolific sample (N=200; Mage=23.06; 40.5% female; 48% racial minorities) was used to establish the norms; a community sample (N=291; Mage=22.40; 59.5% female; 60.5% racial minorities) was used to test the norms out of sample.
Methods: In Sample 1, we developed norms from averaged ratings of 82 ELA items and compared norm-based and self-rating scoring (feasibility test). In Sample 2, we applied Sample 1 norms (replicability test). Dimension scores—threat, deprivation, unpredictability, uncontrollability—predicted cognitive reappraisal, emotion dysregulation, and psychopathology symptoms.
Results: Although discrete events differed in dimensional profiles, cumulative person-level dimensional scores had high co-occurrence (VIFs>100). Norm-based and self-rating scoring produced comparable patterns in Sample 1, replicated in Sample 2. Entered simultaneously, deprivation was the dominant predictor of depression, PTSD, and emotion dysregulation across both samples (R2 = .04-.23, ps < .01) and the only dimension negatively associated with cognitive reappraisal (p = .007).
Conclusions: ELA dimensions are entangled at the person level, preventing clean specificity in naturalistic samples, converging with recent concerns about event-based dimensional approaches. The value of dimensional models may inform sample selection, treat self–norm discrepancies as meaningful appraisal differences, and target such appraisals through interventions.

articles.title: Supervision, Category Structure, and Selective Attention in Category Learning: A Comparative Approach
articles.authors: Hyungwook Yim; Leyre Castro; Jay I. Myung; Edward A. Wasserman; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles.abstract: We investigated the interactions between supervision, category structure, and selective attention in category learning. We compared human adults and pigeons in a category learning task, where we manipulated the category structure (dense vs. sparse) and the level of supervision by corrective feedback (low vs. high). Results showed a benefit of supervision across species, which was particularly strong in learning the sparse categories. Moreover, both species benefitted from category structures that had multiple category-relevant dimensions (i.e., dense categories). In addition, human adults, who have a more advanced ability to attend selectively, showed faster learning and better generalization overall. Finally, attention was optimized to the category-relevant dimension in the sparse category only in human adults. Subsequent computational simulation of the data indicated that these patterns were well explained by a parameter that controls the ability to flexibly switch attention to category-relevant dimensions.

articles.title: The Face of ChatGPT:  Using Reverse Correlation to Explore Mental Representations of AI
articles.authors: Carl Michael Galang; Khaled Hassanein; Milena Head; Sukhvinder S. Obhi
articles.abstract: People readily attribute mental states to large language models like ChatGPT, but the kind of mental representation that is formed when a user imagines such models as a person is unknown. Across two experiments, we used reverse correlation, a data-driven method originally developed in psychophysics, to assess what people think ChatGPT looks like when visualized as a human face. In Phase 1, participants completed a reverse correlation task selecting which of two noisy faces looked most like ChatGPT were it human; in Phase 2, naïve participants rated the resulting classification images (CIs). Across both a female base (Experiment 1) and a male base (Experiment 2) image, ChatGPT CIs were perceived as warmer, more empathetic, and more human-like than the base images, but did not differ reliably on the attributes of competence or knowledge. By revealing the kind of human face people assign to ChatGPT, this study sheds important light on the mental representations relevant to Human-AI interaction. Understanding such representations allows deeper insights into how users come to trust, rely on, and socially engage with artificial agents.

articles.title: A Measurement Framework for Significant Other AI (SO-AI): Development of the SO-AI Questionnaire
articles.authors: Sung Park; Mayu Koike; Yuri Oki; Soyoung Jung; Seohyun Cho
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly evolving from a task-oriented technology into a relational partner that provides emotional support, guidance, companionship, and long-term interaction. Although previous Human–AI relationship research has substantially advanced our understanding of constructs such as trust, anthropomorphism, attachment, empathy, and social presence, existing measurement approaches primarily assess individual psychological characteristics rather than the broader relational role that AI may occupy in people's lives. This conceptual gap has become increasingly important as AI systems become more personalized, persistent, and psychologically meaningful. To address this gap, we introduce the Significant Other AI (SO-AI) Measurement Framework, a multidisciplinary conceptual framework that conceptualizes AI as a potential psychologically significant other through the integration of multiple complementary relational functions. Building upon theories from psychology, sociology, clinical psychology, family therapy, and education, the framework synthesizes recurring relational functions into a unified conceptual model for understanding long-term human–AI relationships. We developed the SO-AI Questionnaire through a theory-driven process involving multidisciplinary literature synthesis, exploratory qualitative investigations, iterative expert panel review, and systematic item refinement. The resulting questionnaire adopts a parallel assessment strategy that evaluates both human significant others and AI systems using corresponding relational dimensions while further incorporating situation-based behavioral scenarios to examine consultation preferences across everyday contexts. By introducing the SO-AI Measurement Framework and Questionnaire, this work provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for future validation studies and research on long-term relational AI.

articles.title: Learning evolution at home: E-books promote evolutionary understanding for elementary school students and their parents
articles.authors: David Menendez
articles.abstract: People across ages and education levels often struggle to understand evolution. Although studies in formal learning settings have examined how interventions influence children’s understanding of evolution, studies in informal learning settings have not explored how these informal interactions influence learning about evolution. In addition to exploring children’s learning from these interactions, we were also interested in whether parents learned, as many adults misunderstand evolution. In this study, we were interested in whether parents and children could learn about evolution by reading picture books at home, and whether features of the book (such as the richness of the visualizations) or their interaction (such as making analogies or extra-textual explanations) while reading would influence learning. From July to October, 2021, we recruited 83 children in first to fourth grade (Age: M = 7.97, SD = 1.10; 33 boys, 46 girls, 1 non-binary) and their parents to complete a two-session online study where they were randomly assigned to read a book about evolution with either detailed or sparse images. The results suggest that both children and parents learned about evolution through a shared book reading activity. Children and parents were also able to generalize from the book to new scenarios. When there was evidence for an effect of visualization, it showed that, contrary to our hypothesis, parents and children showed greater generalization when they read the book with detailed images. Overall, we showed that children and parents can learn complex STEM concepts through informal activities and that contextual factors influenced this learning.

articles.title: HiLex: A quick test to measure lexical proficiency in Hindi
articles.authors: Niket Agrawal; Ark Verma
articles.abstract:
Language proficiency is associated with lexical and semantic access, as well as individual differences, and it also informs models of word recognition. Vocabulary size is also an important predictor in studies of aging and bilingualism. In a recent review Olson (2024), highlighted the importance of robust and objective measures of language proficiency across sub-fields such as psycholinguistics, cognitive linguistics, language development, and pedagogy, rather than relying solely on subjective scales and questionnaires. While objective measures of proficiency are available in several languages, including English, French, Italian, Dutch, Spanish, and Chinese, Hindi has lacked such a measure despite being one of the most widely spoken languages in the world.
In the current study, we propose that HiLex provides a robust, quick and objective measure of individual differences in Hindi proficiency in first- and second-language speakers. The study was based on existing yes/no vocabulary test paradigms. Two experiments were conducted to develop and validate the HiLex test. In the first experiment, 308 native and non-native speakers of Hindi performed a lexical decision task on a pool of 240 words and pseudowords. Item response theory was used to select final subset of 90 items (60 words, 30 pseudowords) for HiLex. The second experiment was conducted independently with 126 participants to validate HiLex scores against multiple dimensions of language proficiency, as well as self-ratings. Results showed that HiLex scores significantly differentiated native from non-native speakers (t(121.6) = 7.22, p < .001) and were highly correlated with other objective measures, including reading comprehension and word meaning (rs > .60). The test is freely accessible, quick to administer, and also aligns with open-science principles.

articles.title: Strengthening the Psychedelic Safety Net: A Call for a Coordinated Ecosystem of Post-Psychedelic Care
articles.authors: Christian Jurlando; Kristin Nash; Dario Jalilzadeh Masah; Jules Evans; Stacy Rush
articles.abstract: As psychedelic use rises globally, a growing subset of individuals experience extended post-psychedelic difficulties (EPPD): persistent adverse reactions including severe anxiety, depersonalization/derealization, persistent insomnia, HPPD, and PTSD-like features. Although a number of non-profit organizations have developed vital support networks, infrastructure remains fragmented, with peer support, integration services, and clinical care operating without shared definitions, triage protocols, or referral pathways, and clinicians capable of treating EPPDs as psychiatric conditions remaining extraordinarily rare. This Perspective Essay maps the existing ecosystem of post-psychedelic care before proposing a coordinated framework organized around three functions—recognition, routing, and learning. We suggest three working categories of psychedelic difficulty (Acute Psychedelic Crisis, Short-term Integration Difficulties, and Extended Post-Psychedelic Difficulties) alongside four coordination pillars: coordinated public-facing presence, common minimal intake, shared learning, and outcome tracking. We argue that voluntary, decentralized coordination among peer, clinical, and research organizations offers a practical path toward a psychedelic safety net capable of caring for those who struggle, not only those who thrive.

articles.title: The temporal architecture of decision regulation: Development and initial validation of the Decision Regulation Inventory
articles.authors: Nicola Thibault; Alana Arrouet; Roxane Hoyer
articles.abstract: Decision regulation fails recurrently across psychiatric and neurological conditions. Theory has long described it as a temporally extended process unfolding across anticipation, real-time control, and post-decision reevaluation, yet existing psychometric tools measure only its fragments, and no single instrument integrates them. We present the Decision Regulation Inventory (DRI), a 24-item self-report instrument that bridges this gap within a single temporal framework, with items grounded in morally consequential scenarios as a prototype of high-stakes choice. In 557 French-speaking adults, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses recovered a five-dimensional structure (Empathic Deliberation, Principled Deliberation, Control Failure under Excitation, Control Failure under Pressure, Post-decision Reevaluation) with acceptable model fit and configural and metric measurement invariance across sex; invariance across country was supported but preliminary given the small French subsample. Convergent and divergent correlations with six external instrument families broadly conformed to the predicted nomological pattern. In exploratory clinical contrasts, Control Failure under Pressure tracked psychiatric and neurological burden, with FDR-corrected elevations in six of seven diagnostic categories, a transdiagnostic signal whose specificity against negative affectivity remains to be tested. Pending discriminant and clinical validation, the DRI offers a process-level instrument for consequential decision research and clinical psychopathology.

articles.title: Between Law and Conscience: Act Legality Shapes Moral Evaluation
articles.authors: Mane Kara-Yakoubian; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles.abstract: Can legality shape moral judgment? Across four experiments (N = 1,559), participants judged identical actions as more morally wrong when they were described as illegal rather than “not illegal.” This effect extended to judgments of moral character: individuals who performed illegal actions were evaluated more negatively than those who performed otherwise identical legal actions. The influence of legality was robust across several contexts, emerging even when agents violated the law unintentionally, when laws were imposed by a totalitarian government, and when actions were described as socially accepted by the majority of local residents. At the same time, legality exerted a stronger influence when it aligned with prevailing social norms and among participants who more strongly endorsed respect for authority as a moral good. We propose that people commonly use legality as a heuristic cue when evaluating the morality of actions and actors. Together, these findings suggest that legal frameworks not only reflect public opinion but also shape how people judge the morality of actions and those who perform them.

articles.title: Effects of Youth First on Student and Teacher Well-Being and Education Outcomes
articles.authors: Peter L. Cooper; Abigail Russo; Katherine S. Leventhal; Emmanuel Sibomana; Theogene Kayiranga; Libby Karangwa-Miles; Steve Leventhal
articles.abstract: This quasi-experimental study examined the effects of Youth First Rwanda, a teacher-facilitated school-based well-being program, on lower secondary students and teachers. The study followed 9,649 students across 100 matched intervention and comparison schools from baseline to endline and eight-month follow-up. Difference-in-differences and cross-sectional mixed-effects models were used to estimate program effects. Youth First Rwanda improved students’ psychosocial knowledge and confidence at endline, and positive effects emerged at eight-month follow-up for emotional resilience, coping, well-being, peer relationships, gender attitudes, school belonging, teacher support, and selected education outcomes. Teachers in intervention schools reported higher psychosocial knowledge, confidence, emotional resilience, and facilitation knowledge. Findings support school-based well-being programming as a scalable strategy for adolescent mental health promotion in Rwanda.

articles.title: Understanding Polarization via the Relationship between Political Attitudes and Partisan Strength
articles.authors: Federico Zimmerman; Mina Cikara; Yphtach Lelkes; Joaquin Navajas; Delia Baldassarri; Mark John Brandt; James Druckman; James Gross; Eran Halperin; Samara Klar
articles.abstract: Political polarization poses a growing threat to democratic governance. We suggest that one overlooked driver of polarization lies in the dynamic relationship between political attitudes and partisan strength. People's attitudes on specific issues and partisan strength are often thought to move together. However, examining the relationship between attitudes and partisan strength among U.S. partisans reveals that they may diverge over time, with attitudes moving toward extremity ahead of partisan strength. This pattern is particularly clear among self-identified moderate partisans, who increasingly adopt extreme attitudes over time while initially still identifying as moderate partisans. We call this phenomenon attitude acrophily (attraction to extreme attitudes): the tendency to be attracted to extreme political attitudes. Using American National Election Studies data, we show that by 2020, moderate Democrats and Republicans were more likely to report extreme attitudes on health insurance, guaranteed jobs, and aid to Black Americans than to report moderate attitudes. Furthermore, panel data analysis, tracking the same partisans over eight years, shows that the rise in attitude acrophily is not the result of generational replacement. We also show that attitude acrophily has important implications, as moderate partisans with extreme attitudes are more likely to report greater partisan strength over time. This framework suggests that polarization evolves first through shifts in attitudes and then in partisan strength. Understanding this sequence points to pathways for preventing further escalation.

articles.title: Reduced Mental Health and Wellbeing in Parents of Transgender Youth Following the 2025 U.S. Presidential Inauguration
articles.authors: Rachel Leshin; NA; Grey Raber; Natalie Gallagher; Kristina Olson
articles.abstract: The numerous executive orders directed at transgender youth in the weeks following the 2025 U.S. presidential inauguration were likely a signal to these youth—and their parents—that the federal government no longer supported them. Using a longitudinal design spanning three years prior to the inauguration (2022-2024) and two months surrounding the inauguration, we tested whether the mental health and wellbeing of U.S.-based transgender youth and their parents declined relative to that of cisgender youth and their parents in a sample that, on the whole, did not support the new administration (N=160 youth, 12-17 years; N=167 parents). Across preregistered analyses, we observed significant declines in the mental health and wellbeing of parents of transgender youth vs. parents of cisgender youth; we observed fewer differences over time between transgender vs. cisgender youth themselves. Our findings identify an immediate potential cost of the current political environment for supportive parents of transgender youth.

articles.title: Frustrative nonreward engages midfrontal theta power and modulates effort expenditure
articles.authors: Nellia Bellaert; Federico Cassioli; Wan-Ling Tseng; Mandy Rossignol
articles.abstract: Aim: Irritability, defined as an increased propensity to experience frustration, was associated with reduced willingness to expend effort for rewards at the self-reported level. However, the effect of frustration on effort expenditure has rarely been experimentally tested in humans. To address this gap, this study introduced a frustration induction in the Effort-Doors task to elicit frustrative nonreward (FNR), a negative emotional state triggered by unexpected reward loss, and examined its effects on physical effort expenditure and feedback-related electroencephalographic (EEG) activity. We also tested whether these effects vary as a function of state and trait measures of motivation and affect. Methods: Linear mixed-effects models tested the effects of FNR induction on self-reported, behavioral, and EEG measures in young adults (N=83) completing the novel Frustrative Effort-Doors task. Models tested manipulation effects, trial-level post-feedback adjustment, and moderation by state and trait measures. Midfrontal theta power (MFθ) was extracted using multivariate spatial filtering and examined as a function of feedback (win vs. FNR), effort (low vs. high), and subsequent behavioral adjustments. Results: The frustration induction decreased self-reported state motivation and increased state frustration, arousal, and response speed. MFθ was enhanced following FNR feedback and was further modulated by state frustration, particularly during high-effort trials. Higher state frustration was associated with reduced response vigor during effort execution following FNR feedback. MFθ did not predict trial-to-trial behavioral adjustments. Discussion: These findings indicate that FNR recruits MFθ, a neural marker of cognitive control, whereas individual differences in state frustration modulates physical effort execution following unexpected reward loss.

articles.title: Thermal pain tolerance depends on stimulus duration and thermode type
articles.authors: Yi Wei; Julie S.P. Storkson; Kai Sherwood; Maya Joshi Delity; Titilola Akintola; Troy C. Dildine; Hayley Owens; Lauren Yvette Atlas
articles.abstract:
Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST) allows researchers and clinicians to evaluate variations in acute pain and thermosensation within and across individuals. However, it is unclear how experimental factors, such as thermode type and stimulation duration, affect pain measurements. We compared three types of thermodes at two stimulus durations to assess potential impacts on QST outcomes.

Across two experiments, a total of 83 (45 and 38 respectively) healthy volunteers each completed two QST tasks that varied in thermode type (ATS, CHEPS or T03) and/or stimulus duration (8s or 3s), with order counterbalanced across participants. In each task, heat was applied to 8 sites on the left volar forearm for three runs (24 trials in total) and temperatures were selected through an adaptive staircase calibration procedure. Pain threshold, tolerance, and the strength of the correlation between stimulus temperature and pain ratings (r²) were estimated using linear regression. 

Results indicate that briefer stimuli were associated with higher pain tolerance (t = -3.28, p = 0.018), while there was no effect of duration on threshold or temperature-rating correlation. Thermode type influenced pain tolerance in short (3s) (t = -3.10, p = 0.01) but not long (8s) durations, such that on 3s trials, tolerance was higher with the smaller surface thermode (T03) compared to the larger surface thermode (CHEPS), consistent with spatial summation. No sex differences were found. These results demonstrate that suprathreshold pain tolerance, but not threshold, is sensitive to stimulus duration and thermode type. These findings also indicate the importance of methodological standardization in QST and the careful selection of suprathreshold pain stimuli in experiment design.

articles.title: When Takeovers Require Cognitive Control: Effects of Partial Automation and Cognitive Load on Driver-Initiated Responses to Traffic Hazards on Urban Roads
articles.authors: Hao Qin; Rafael C. Gonçalves; Courtney Michael Goodridge; Natasha Merat
articles.abstract: Partially automated driving (PAD) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in consumer vehicles. While drivers are obliged to monitor the roadway and the system during PAD, they do not always comply with this requirement and may engage in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs). Literature has emphasized the detrimental effects of visual–manual NDRTs on drivers’ capability to takeover control from PAD while reporting negligible effects of non-visual NDRTs (e.g., hands-free phone calls) and cognitive load. However, most studies focused on alerted scenarios, with takeover requests lowering drivers’ reliance on anticipation and cognitive load, masking the effects of cognitive load. Related work also examined PAD conditions alone, neglecting the combined effects of automation and cognitive load on drivers’ responses. To address the gaps, we conducted a driving simulator study examining the influence of cognitive load, induced by a 2-back task, on driver-initiated responses to urban traffic hazards (e.g., crossing pedestrians, oncoming vehicles) during both manual driving and PAD. The timing and quality of driver-initiated responses were analysed separately for each hazard with detail. Results showed that driver-initiated responses during PAD were less anticipatory and relied more on cognitive control. This shift led to higher situational criticality and heightened susceptibility of responses to cognitive load during PAD. Hazard characteristics such as motion speed and cue ambiguity appeared to influence cognitive load effects and warrant systematic examination in future work. Together, these findings underscore an elevated safety risk associated with cognitive load during PAD, especially in scenarios requiring cognitively demanding, driver-initiated intervention.

articles.title: The Impact of Partial Automation and Cognitive Load on Drivers’ Visual Search Strategies in an Urban Driving Environment
articles.authors: Hao Qin; Rafael C. Gonçalves; Courtney Michael Goodridge; Natasha Merat
articles.abstract: Non-visual cognitive tasks (e.g., hands-free phone conversations) are well known to impair drivers’ visual search in manual driving, but evidence in partially automated driving (PAD) remains inconsistent and limited, especially in complex driving environments that demand active visual scanning. In a driving-simulator study, we examined how automation and cognitive load (2-back task) shape visual-search strategies in a busy urban setting with frequent distractors and potential hazards, using both temporal and sequential scanning measures. Unlike findings from monotonous driving contexts, PAD drivers broadened their visual search without trading off attention to the forward road. Under cognitive load, their attention to peripheral roadway declined more sharply than in manual driving, leading to restricted visual search across both driving modes. Our results underscore the influence of non-visual distraction on drivers’ visual scanning during PAD in complex environments and highlight the value of eye-tracking–based features for monitoring cognitive load.

articles.title: Psychometric properties of the Brazilian version of the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire
articles.authors: Tally L. Tafla; Paulo Guirro Laurence; Priscilla Brandi Gomes Godoy; Juliana P Bruckner; Laura Hull; William Mandy; Elizabeth Shephard
articles.abstract: To adapt to social expectations and gain peer acceptance, autistic individuals may engage in compensatory behaviors, known as camouflaging, which has been associated with mental health outcomes including depression and anxiety. Instruments that accurately measure camouflaging in autistic individuals are therefore important. The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q) is widely used in literature and shows good psychometric properties. However, most non-English-speaking countries such as Brazil, lack validated instruments to assess camouflaging behaviours. The present study reports the adaptation of the CAT-Q for Brazil and examines the psychometric properties of its Brazilian version. The translation and cultural adaptation had independent translations and evaluation by expert judges, including autistic adults. A total of 923 autistic and 470 non-autistic adults from across Brazil completed the CAT-Q-BR and the Autism Quotient–Short Version (AQ-10). Confirmatory factor analyses tested the original three-factor structure of the CAT-Q-BR; Convergent validity was examined through associations with autistic traits on the AQ-10 and self-reported anxiety and depression diagnoses and known-groups validity (gender differences) were also analyzed. Results supported the original structure, with acceptable model fit (CFI = 0.964, TLI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.076, SRMR = 0.066) and internal consistency for total score was good (α = 0.88). No significant association was found between CAT-Q-BR and the AQ-10. However, higher camouflaging scores were significantly associated with self-reported anxiety and depression. Gender-diverse participants reported higher camouflaging compared to cisgender men and women. Overall, findings provide initial evidence supporting the CAT-Q-BR as a reliable measure of camouflaging behaviors in Brazilian adults.

articles.title: The role of interoceptive body trusting in the link between trauma, resilience, mental health and somatic symptoms in children
articles.authors: Megan Klabunde; Giulia Poerio; Helge Gillmeister
articles.abstract: Trauma is a well established contributor to mental health difficulties and somatisation in children. Prior research has largely focused on cognitive pathways, neglecting bodily mechanisms that may influence psychological development. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether interoceptive awareness—the conscious perception of internal bodily signals—serves as a mechanistic link between trauma exposure and subsequent mental health, resilience, and somatic outcomes. Sixty five children recruited from local schools completed self report questionnaires assessing interoceptive awareness, mental health status, resilience, and somatic symptoms, alongside a trauma screener and a structured clinical interview for trauma if exposure was detected. Results indicated that interoceptive body trusting significantly predicted mental health, resilience, and somatic symptomatology. Moreover, interoceptive body trusting mediated the relationship between childhood trauma symptoms and both mental health and somatic outcomes, suggesting that interoceptive body trusting may be a pivotal mechanism by which trauma influences psychopathology and somatic symptoms in youth.

articles.title: Covariation among higher-order psychopathology dimensions is driven by nomorbidity, not comorbidity
articles.authors: Ashley L. Watts; Adon Rosen; Ashley Lauren Greene; Kevin Michael King; Francisco Agustin Calvache Meyer; Timothy J Trull; Kenneth J. Sher; Keanan Joyner
articles.abstract: Emerging classification frameworks claim that covariation among psychopathology dimensions reflects comorbidity. We scrutinized this claim by applying Bayesian change point models to four waves of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data (N = 11,868 youths) and examined associations among higher-order psychopathology dimensions. Covariation between psychopathology dimensions was driven by nomorbidity, not comorbidity: We observed strong positive associations among psychopathology dimensions at relatively extreme low (asymptomatic) levels (e.g., when 3 to 5 symptoms were endorsed) and weak positive associations at higher levels. For instance, at wave 1, a 1-point increase in internalizing was associated with a 32% increase in externalizing at nearly asymptomatic levels (B = .28), compared to only a 7% increase at higher levels (B = .07). These findings challenge existing assumptions about comorbidity in non-clinical samples, suggesting that covariation is more accurately explained by the absence of symptomatology rather than shared psychiatric conditions.

articles.title: Insegnare parole concrete e astratte alla tua bambina/o: un compito interattivo con le famiglie
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Questo studio indaga il processo di trasmissione ed acquisizione di conoscenze relative a concetti astratti e concreti (ad esempio, fantasia vs. barca) attraverso un paradigma interattivo. Tredici famiglie, ciascuna con un figlio o una figlia, hanno partecipato a un compito di definizione concettuale basato sul paradigma clinico Lausanne Trilogue Play. I genitori, prima individualmente e poi insieme, hanno spiegato ai propri figli concetti astratti e concreti. Sono stati analizzati i gesti prodotti allo scopo di verificare l'ipotesi che gesti diversi possano accompagnare la trasmissione di concetti astratti e concreti. I risultati indicano che i gesti variano in funzione del tipo di concetto e del ruolo familiare (madre, padre, figlio/a), e che il tipo di concetto modula la struttura delle co-occorrenze gestuali; l'effetto differenziale tra concetti astratti e concreti sulla produzione gestuale, inizialmente marcato, tende tuttavia ad attenuarsi nel corso dell'interazione. I risultati sono rilevanti per le teorie che sottolineano l’importanza della relazione tra l’astrattezza e l’interazione sociale.

articles.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Claudia Mazzuca; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

articles.title: Towards an Active Inference Personality Framework: The Deep-Self Predictive Cascade Model
articles.authors: Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract: Contemporary personality science rests on robust descriptive taxonomies, such as the Big-5, that catalogue how individuals differ but remain largely silent on why these differences arise and structure as they do. We introduce the Deep-Self Predictive Cascade Model, a conceptual framework that recasts personality in the language of active inference. Personality is modelled not as an inventory of traits but as the topography of an agent's expected free energy landscape: a set of attractor basins whose depth and location are set by deep prior beliefs and precision-allocation strategies. We describe a four-level hierarchy that cascades from six foundational Ultra-Priors, governing the agent's epistemic, allostatic, and teleological imperatives, through three Core Affective States and six Precision Biases that allocate resources across the minimal, agentic, and narrative self-models, to the observable phenotypes catalogued by trait taxonomy. This parameter space provides a common vocabulary onto which major cybernetic, affective, and clinical frameworks can be mapped. We present a proof-of-concept simulation provides evidence that the cascade's topology is capable of reproducing the empirical covariance structure of the Big-5, as well as a set of falsifiable predictions to test and refine our proposal.

articles.title: Defining Developmental Language Disorder and Dyslexia in Schools: A Mixed Methods Analysis
articles.authors: Timothy DeLuca; Katharine Radville; Danika L. Pfeiffer; Tiffany P. Hogan; Christie Davis
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Interprofessional practice requires regular communication between professionals from different disciplines using shared terminology. Within schools, many professionals are tasked with supporting children with language disorders, namely DLD and/or dyslexia. Limited information exists as to (1) how school-based professionals’ definitions of DLD and dyslexia align with research definitions, (2) how different school-based professionals define language disorders, (3) how school-based professionals’ definitions of DLD and dyslexia align across professional groups, and (4) how one’s definition of a language disorder correlates with other measures of knowledge.
Methods: In this mixed-methods study, we analyzed 304 definitions of language disorders from school-based professionals using a summative content analysis process. We explored the relationship between definitions and knowledge of disorder characteristics and best practices.
Results: Data reflected limited alignment between professional and research definitions of DLD and dyslexia. Common misconceptions related to each disorder were prevalent among school-based professionals’ definitions. There were differences between the extent to which professional groups’ definitions aligned with research definitions of DLD and dyslexia.
Conclusion: Results highlight the need for shared terminology between professional groups and researchers to improve collaborative practices and to narrow the research to practice gap.  
 Keywords: DLD; dyslexia; interprofessional collaboration

articles.title: Racial-Ethnic and Gender Inequities in School Absences, Exclusions and SEND Responses to Mental Health Need in Pathways to Youth Justice: Population-based Cohort Study in England
articles.authors: Sorcha Ní Chobhthaigh; Josephine Musanu; Camille Cox; Twyla Greenway-Bailey; Cyra Neave; Mina Mawi; Amie Buhari; Mel Green; Aqsa Suleman; Rochelle Ann Burgess
articles.abstract:
Background: School absences and exclusions represent indicators of unmet need, associated with mental health difficulties and justice involvement. Racial-ethnic and gender inequities in Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND) provision for Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs in response to these indicators risk perpetuating long-term health, education and justice inequalities. Understanding how these systems interact offers insight into critical junctures where equitable responses could prevent escalating need and criminalisation. 
Methods: In partnership with young people and community stakeholders, we analysed population-level linked school and police administrative data for 3.7m children (born 1997-2003) who attended state schools in England.  We examined absence and exclusion rates, timing, and risk ratios for pathways between different sequences of need indicators, SEND-for-SEMH and youth justice contacts.
Results: Most pupils with youth justice contacts had experienced an exclusion (boys: 77.2%; girls: 70.6%), rising to over 85% for boys and 80% for girls from Black Caribbean and Mixed White-Black Caribbean backgrounds. Indicators clustered between 11-14 years, with younger exclusions for Black Caribbean, Mixed White-Black, Romani and Irish Traveller boys. Systematic racial-ethnic and gender differences were evident in pathways between indicators, SEND-for-SEMH and youth justice contacts. For pupils with SEND-for-SEMH, the relative risk of youth justice contacts was higher for those with subsequent severe absence (boys: 2.0, girls: 2.6) and exclusion (boys: 4.2, girls: 6.5), which varied by racial-ethnic group.
Conclusions: Intersectional discrimination in school responses to need - manifesting in harmful disciplinary practices and failures to enable engagement in education - fuels cycles of unmet mental health need and youth justice contact. Differential and harmful responses to children’s needs based on gender and racial-ethnic group breach Public Sector Equality and Safeguarding Duties. A co-ordinated multi-system public health approach is urgently required, improving equitable access to care, addressing discriminatory policing practices, and immediate commitment to cease exclusions.

articles.title: Social Learning Undermines Performance and Increases Inequality When Decision Outcomes Depend on Prior Success
articles.authors: Paul K. Bergmann; Dominik Deffner
articles.abstract: Individuals often estimate the risks and benefits of decision alternatives from their own experiences and the behaviours and outcomes of others. In both simulations and experiments, social learning has largely been found to improve decision-making compared to individual learning alone. While previous work treated decision outcomes over repeated choices as independent, in many real-life contexts, including financial investments, life-course developments, or social networks, decision outcomes depend on previous outcomes, producing self-reinforcing ``the-rich-get-richer" dynamics. The adaptive consequences of social learning under such dependent, multiplicative conditions remain unknown. Using social reinforcement learning models in an agent-based simulation framework, we identify diverging effects of several well-established social learning strategies. In contrast to independent, additive environments, nearly all forms of social learning in multiplicative environments undermined performance and increased inequality  compared to individual learning. This occurred because an overly risk-seeking but fortunate minority provided systematically misleading cues. Payoff-biased learning strategies, usually considered a safeguard against herding, further deteriorated decision-quality, whereas conformity-biased copying slightly improved performance. These findings were observed even under time-optimal utility transformations of private and social payoff information. Together, our findings demonstrate disadvantageous collective learning under stochastic multiplicative growth, emphasizing that nearly all forms of social influence exacerbate inequality in these systems.

articles.title: From disorder to neurotype? Exploring a neurodiversity-affirming take on the autism diagnostic label.
articles.authors: Gert-Jan Vanaken
articles.abstract:
Autism is increasingly claimed to be a neurotype, an expression of human neurodiversity, rather than a disorder. In this Community Perspective, I explore the implications of this paradigm shift for autism as a clinical diagnosis. Can a non-pathologising, yet clinically meaningful alternative to the current diagnostic label be envisioned?
To ground this exploration empirically, I synthesise qualitative findings of how autistic individuals and their relatives experience the current diagnostic label in practice. Drawing on the disease–illness–sickness triad, I evaluate these experiences from clinical, personal, and societal perspectives, highlighting the current label’s multifunctional but ambivalent nature.
I then introduce and critically assess three alternatives to the current label: elimination, clinical case formulation, and self-identification. Each addresses certain shortcomings of the existing label, but none preserves the full range of its functional value.
Finally, I outline a proposal for a revised, neurodiversity-affirming diagnostic label. Two core reforms are advanced: [1] a co-produced reformulation of diagnostic criteria, integrating first-person perspectives and reducing deficit-based language; and [2] the replacement of the impairment criterion with a contextualised assessment of person–environment mismatch.
I hope this Community Perspective can help to stimulate further discussion on the future of the autism diagnostic label.

articles.title: The Effect of Psychological Distance on Level of Construal: What do we Learn from the CLIMR Failed Replication?
articles.authors: Nira Liberman; Ori Levit-Mor
articles.abstract: Calderon and her colleagues (2026) failed to replicate Constural Level Theory’s (CLT, Liberman & Trope, 2014; Trope & Liberman, 2010) finding that psychologically more distant actions—actions that are planned for the more distant future, for more distant places, for less likely situations and those performed by more socially distant persons- are construed more abstractly. There is considerable evidence for the effect of psychological distance on construal level, including recent, well-powered, preregistered studies. There is also a theory behind this effect: Higher-level constructs change less over distance. So why did the replication fail? What can we learn from it about (studying) distance and level-of-construal, and more generally, about multi-lab replications? This commentary suggests that in several respects, the replication project fell short of meeting established standards of psychological research. The results of the project are partly based on samples that included many inattentive participants, on responders who were not native speakers of the language in which the experiment was presented, on translations that did not preserve the original intent of the materials, on manipulations of distance that were confusing, weak, or confounded with valence and on manipulation-checks that did not check the actual manipulations. The commentary also offers a re-analysis of some of Calderon and colleagues’ (2026) data and a new replication study, both of which show an effect of temporal distance on construal level. Finally, we suggest two ways in which the Registered Replication Report format may be improved.

articles.title: Why dream amnesia may be adaptive:  dream recall frequency predicts dream-reality confusion
articles.authors: Sofia Tzioridou; Leonore Bovy; Sebastian Sattler; Martin Dresler
articles.abstract: Dreaming is a universal phenomenon, yet the ability to recall dream content varies among individuals and most dreams are forgotten quickly after waking up. Such dream amnesia seems paradoxical given the proposed adaptive functions of dreaming. It has been theorized that dream amnesia might serve an evolutionary adaptive function, protecting against cognitive disruptions such as dream-reality confusion. The present study tested this hypothesis by examining the association between dream recall frequency and dream-reality confusion. By analysing data from 4,961 adults participating in a population-based survey, we show that more frequent dream recall is associated with a higher likelihood of dream-reality confusion. The association held after controlling for age, sex, and lucid dreaming frequency. Moreover, individuals with higher dream recall frequency were also more likely to report dream-reality confusion experiences as more personally relevant and disruptive to daily functioning. We propose that while dreaming may support implicit learning processes (e.g., social or threat simulation), limiting explicit recall of dream content may help maintain a clear distinction between internally generated and externally experienced events. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the functional role of memory processes in dreaming. However, longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to determine whether dream amnesia plays a protective causal role.

articles.title: Running in Tight Spaces: A Large-scale Assessment of Physical and Psychological Safety Risks in Freely Moving Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Lukas Kornemann; Yonatan Hutabarat; Huaiyu Liu; Max Christian Pensel; Ulises Daniel Serratos Hernandez; Juliana Katharina Sporrer; Sajjad Zabbah; Dominik R Bach
articles.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used to study human behavior in ecologically valid, embodied environments, but its physical and psychological risks beyond cybersickness remain poorly quantified. In this observational study, we provide a safety assessment of freely moving VR (fm-VR), using data from 859 participants in low-speed (<1 m/s) and higher-speed (>3 m/s) experiments. We show that a prominent accident risk factor, play area breach, is governed mainly by virtual environment design and to a small extent by room size, whereas ensuing collisions are predicted by the physical safety buffer, and falls by postural demands during rapid locomotion. At the moment of a breach, participants showed no kinematic evidence of representing the physical boundary, a mechanism likely to generalize to augmented and mixed reality. We develop and validate a kinematic model that predicts collision risk from limited pilot data and enables safety buffer optimization. Applying these combined design principles, the last experiment in our set achieved the highest peak locomotion speeds with no collisions. Psychological risk was low: dropout due to distress was rare (< 1%), intrusive memories following distressing virtual scenarios were comparable to those reported in the trauma film paradigm, and cybersickness fell below published reference means. Together, these findings show that fm-VR can be conducted safely through coordinated design, and provide a general, quantitative, and publicly available basis for risk assessment applicable across embodied and extended-reality research.

articles.title: At What Sample Size Do Correlations Stabilise? On Unicorns and Other Improbable Creatures
articles.authors: Anthony Durand; Clément Guichet
articles.abstract: To ensure sufficient statistical power, researchers are encouraged to justify their sample size through power analysis (Lakens, 2022; Cohen, 1988). One complementary approach estimates the required sample size based on the stability of the anticipated effect δ (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). However, this approach was originally developed assuming normal distributions, and no simulation studies have examined its robustness under non-normal data. We therefore conducted simulations following Schönbrodt and Perugini's (2013) procedure to estimate the point of stability across various non-normal distributions. Results indicated that small-to-moderate normality violations only slightly affected the point of stability, whereas strong violations produced substantial changes. Implications are discussed.

articles.title: Beyond Labels: Data-Derived Profiles Better Describe Children and Young People’s Needs in Education
articles.authors: Jo Hutchinson; Emre Deniz; Megan Frith; Kathryn Asbury; Dianne Newbury; Umar Toseeb
articles.abstract: Background. Children and young people (CYP) with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) have poorer outcomes compared with those without SEND. It remains unclear how to best identify CYP with SEND. We examined whether profiles of CYP needs align with SEND identification and whether they discriminate young adult outcomes better than current SEND identification. Methods. We analysed data from three population-based cohorts in England: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (N = 15,645); Millennium Cohort Study (N = 18,827); Twins Early Development Study (N = 7,859). We fitted latent mixture models to data on social and behavioural, emotional, and cognitive functioning. We did this separately for each cohort at three developmental stages: early childhood (age 3-5 years); middle childhood (age 7-9 years); adolescence (age 13-18 years). We ran logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses to determine whether data-derived sub-groups discriminate young adult outcomes better than SEND identification. Results. There were CYP with similar profiles of strengths and challenges: typically developing; global difficulties; cognitive difficulties; and social, emotional, behavioural difficulties. Up to a third of CYP experienced difficulties at two or more developmental stages, indicating high levels of persistent educational need in England. SEND identification only partially overlapped with the data-derived sub-groups. Agreement was highest for global and cognitive difficulty sub-groups and lowest for emotional difficulties sub-groups. Difficulty sub-groups showed consistent associations across a range of young adult outcomes. Data-derived sub-groups discriminated university degree attainment, receipt of state benefits, anti-social behaviour, and mental health outcomes better than SEND identification, whereas SEND identification performed better only for GCSE attainment. Conclusions. Current SEND identification only partially captures underlying persistent educational need in England. Descriptive profiles of CYP’s strengths and challenges are likely to be a better alternative to the current SEND system for identifying CYP at risk of poor outcomes post compulsory education.

articles.title: Tailoring Personality Interventions: How Timing, Context, and Strategies Influence Proximal Intervention Outcomes
articles.authors: Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Till Lubczyk; Rosalie Andrae; Eva Asselmann; Susanne Buecker; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Personality interventions are a field of growing interest, as many people want to change aspects of their personality and as such personality changes may positively impact important life outcomes. Although initial research shows that personality interventions can be successful in eliciting lasting trait changes, the strategies, timing, and context of effective personality interventions remain unclear.
