A careful examination of how these characteristics predict intervention effectiveness would advance theoretical models of volitional personality change. We used intensive longitudinal data from the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) Study, a smartphone intervention study designed to decrease participants’ neuroticism that combines experience sampling methods and mobile sensing (N = 399; nobs = 38,275; Mage = 25.48 years; 85% female; 47% living in Switzerland). Using these data, we examined the effects of different intervention strategies and their timing and situational context on the proximal intervention outcomes of intervention adherence, satisfaction, and changes in momentary positive affect. Intervention strategies that targeted the state level of neuroticism had more positive effects on people’s momentary affect than habit-level strategies, providing novel insights into the mechanisms of successful personality change. Furthermore, effects differed depending on the timing and situational context of intervention prompts, highlighting possibilities of optimizing the timing of personality interventions. For example, people were more likely to respond to intervention prompts in quieter environments. Together, these findings inform theoretical models of personality trait change and can be used to guide the development of effective and refined personality interventions.

articles.title: The Manifestation of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
articles.authors: Dean Fido; Sophie Williams; David Sheffield
articles.abstract: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is an endocrine condition associated with physical (e.g., ache, hair loss) and mental (e.g., depression, anxiety, suicidal-ideation) health complications, which, combined with atypical emotional regulation can result in non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) and suicidal intent. This cross-sectional investigation assessed whether NSSI type, onset age, duration, and severity differed between women who did (n = 113; WPCOS) and did not (n = 305; WoPCOS) self-report PCOS, and whether distinct typologies of NSSI were present. Participants completed demographic questions and a measure of NSSI. Comparative analyses indicated that WPCOS women reported a greater propensity to cut and scratch, but not other NSSIs. In women who engaged in NSSI, self-reported PCOS neither impacted onset age, duration, or severity of NSSI. Cluster analysis indicated three typologies of NSSI engagement: ‘Scar-deriving’, ‘Nil-to-low engagers’, and ‘Intensive engagers’. Implications for healthcare providers working with women with PCOS are discussed; there is a need for the provision of NSSI- and emotion regulation-related education on an international scale.

articles.title: State, Trait and Recovery-Related Differences in Reinforcement Learning and Value-Based Decision Making in Major Depressive Disorder
articles.authors: Madeleine Moses-Payne; Ruibin Zhang; Anahit Mkrtchian; Vincent Valton; Alan Gray; Karel Kieslich; Samantha VanUrk; Veronika Samborska; Don Chamith Halahakoon; Peter Dayan
articles.abstract:
Importance

Altered reinforcement learning and decision-making under uncertainty have been implicated in major depressive disorder. However, it remains unclear whether these alterations reflect vulnerability or state effects of active depression, and which behaviours support sustained recovery after remission.

Objective

To dissociate state-like, trait-like, and remission-related alterations in reinforcement learning and value-based decision making in depression.

Design, Setting, and Participants

Unmedicated adults (N=195) were recruited between 2013 and 2019, including individuals with current depression (n=49), individuals remitted from depression (n=50), first-degree non-depressed relatives of individuals with depression (n=36), and healthy controls (n=60).

Main Outcomes and Measures

Participants completed a 4-armed bandit (4AB) reinforcement learning task under volatile uncertainty and a gambling task assessing value-based decision making under risk. Computational parameters indexing reward and punishment learning rates, outcome sensitivity, and decision noise (4AB), and risk aversion, loss aversion, and inverse temperature (gambling) were estimated using hierarchical Bayesian modelling with Bayesian model averaging. Group differences and associations with symptom dimensions derived from confirmatory factor analysis were examined.

Results

Participants were 68.7% female, mean age=27.3 (SD=8.9). Punishment learning rate differed significantly across groups (F₍3,191₎=5.43, p=.001), driven by lower punishment learning rate in the remitted participants compared with all other groups. The remitted group also had lower lapse rates, indicating less random choice (F₍3,191₎=4.37, p=.005). By contrast, in the gambling task depressed and at-risk participants had higher inverse temperature relative to controls (F₍3,191₎=2.93, p=.03), suggesting more consistent use of values to guide choices. Reward and punishment sensitivity (4AB) and risk and loss aversion (gambling) did not differ across groups. Among non-depressed participants, lower punishment learning rates were associated with greater apathy (r=-0.18, p=.033) and anhedonia (r=-0.18, p=.035).

Conclusions and Relevance

These findings suggest a dissociation between state-, trait-, and recovery-associated computational phenotypes in depression. Reduced learning from negative outcomes appears specific to remitted depression, possibly reflecting adaptive changes that support sustained recovery without medication. Computational measures of learning dynamics may help clarify mechanisms of recovery and inform targets for treatment and relapse prevention.

articles.title: Depth Before Strategy: Temporal Choice-History Signatures Reveal Reduced Recursive Social Planning in Autism
articles.authors: Tahmineh Godazgar; Rana Ghamari; Abolfazl Nadi; Atiye Sarabi-Jamab
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is clinically defined through differences in social communication, interaction, and behavioral flexibility, yet the instruments used to detect it rarely capture the trial-by-trial dynamics through which social adaptation unfolds. Here we ask a deliberately methodological question: when autistic participants and healthy controls adapt to a repeated social interaction, does the diagnostically relevant signal live in the cognitive strategy they are inferred to use, or in the temporal structure of their choices? We tested this in a repeated hide-and-seek task in which autistic participants and healthy controls performed the same two-choice decision problem under social and non-social framing and against artificial opponents of graded sophistication. We compared three readings of the same behavior: aggregate performance summaries, Bayesian model-based estimates of latent strategy use, and model-free choice-sequence history kernels measuring how current choices depended on recent self-actions and opponent actions. Aggregate behavior showed context-specific, rather than global, ASD-HC differences. Bayesian model selection revealed condition-dependent shifts in inferred strategy distributions, especially in first-order opponent conditions, where healthy controls were more often assigned to adaptive opponent-modeling strategies and autistic participants to simpler heuristic policies. However, these strategy summaries carried limited individual-level group information. In contrast, choice-history kernels preserved a robust temporal signature. Autistic participants showed stronger immediate self-history dependence in simpler opponent conditions, whereas healthy controls showed stronger lag-2 self-history and opponent-history dependence when the opponent required adaptive tracking. Fixed lag 1:8 kernel features outperformed behavioral and model-based task-derived representations in ASD-HC classification, while clinical variables remained the strongest reference representation. These findings suggest that the clinically relevant variation in repeated social adaptation resides less in a categorical shift between latent strategies than in the temporal organization of choice history. Model-free history kernels thus provide an interpretable complement to generative modeling for computational phenotyping in ASD, situating the present findings within a broader computational framework linking recursive Theory-of-Mind reasoning and individual differences in the depth of social planning that have already proven useful as phenotyping markers in other populations.

articles.title: People Using a Foreign Language Think and Decide Worse, Not Better
articles.authors: Michal Bialek; Rafał Muda; Wojciech Milczarski
articles.abstract: People using a foreign language often decide differently than in their native tongue, a pattern usually read as enhanced rationality. We propose the opposite. Foreign language disrupts metacognitive monitoring, the ability to detect conflict between competing intuitions and to recognise when reflection is needed. We tested this in two experiments with over 1,500 proficient bilinguals solving base rate neglect tasks in their native or foreign language, and measured conflict detection through confidence ratings. Foreign language weakened conflict detection and impaired accuracy, either by failing to engage reflection when needed or by triggering deliberation on problems that did not require it. The effects generalised across three language pairs. The apparent foreign language advantage in reducing bias arises from testing only the trick problems, which masks a broader disruption of the processes that allocate cognitive effort. Foreign language does not improve rationality. It degrades the system that decides when to reflect.

articles.title: The impact of online hate speech and rage bait on social media fatigue in Greece: Evidence from a national cross-sectional study
articles.authors: Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Ioannis Moisoglou; Parisis Gallos; Panagiota Peleka; Olga Galani; Maria Tsiachri; Antigoni Kolisiati; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To examine the impact of online hate speech and rage bait on social media fatigue in general population. Moreover we examined the impact of sociodemographic characteristics on social media fatigue. METHOD A cross-sectional study was conducted in Greece employing an online survey methodology. Data collection took place between February and June 2026 through a structured questionnaire developed and distributed using Google Forms. The survey was disseminated via social media platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. Eligibility criteria required participants to: (a) be aged 18 years or older, (b) possess at least one active account on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, or YouTube, and (c) provide informed consent before participation. We used the Social Media Fatigue Scale-3 items to measure levels of social media fatigue in our sample. RESULTS A total of 1331 individuals participated in the study. More than half of the participants (58.8%) experienced high levels of social media fatigue. Multivariable model identified a positive association between hate speech victimization on social media and social media fatigue (adjusted beta = 0.355; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.190 to 0.520; p < 0.001). Additionally, exposure on hate speech on social media as a bystander was associated with increased social media fatigue (adjusted beta = 0.418; 95% CI: 0.264 to 0.572; p < 0.001). Also, higher levels of engagement in rage bait on social media were significantly associated with higher levels of social media fatigue (adjusted beta = 0.296; 95% CI: 0.157 to 0.435; p < 0.001). We found that reduced age is associated with increased levels social media fatigue (adjusted coefficient beta = -0.050, 95% CI = -0.063 to -0.036, p < 0.001). In other words, younger participants showed higher levels of social media fatigue. Additionally, after adjustment for cofounders we identified a negative association between financial status and social media fatigue (adjusted coefficient beta = -0.140, 95% CI = -0.246 to -0.034, p = 0.010). Also, females experienced higher levels of social media fatigue compared to males (adjusted coefficient beta = 0.690, 95% CI = 0.316 to 1.065, p < 0.001) CONCLUSIONS Hate speech, rage bait, gender, age, and financial status affect social media fatigue. These findings emphasize the potentially detrimental impact of harmful online experiences on individuals’ well-being. Given their potential psychological consequences, including social media fatigue, these findings underscore the importance of developing targeted interventions and preventive strategies aimed at promoting safer, healthier, and more supportive digital environments. Such efforts may contribute to mitigating the adverse effects of harmful online content and enhancing users’ overall online experiences and psychological well-being.

articles.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
articles.authors: Elise Mockett; Matt N Williams; Dianne Gardner; Larry Paing
articles.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

articles.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
articles.authors: Kohei Kajikawa; Shinnosuke Isono
articles.abstract: Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has utilized Node Count, the number of structure-building steps executed at each word, to investigate how the effort invested in structure building affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. Seeking the source of this disagreement, we analyze information-theoretic measures and reading times using three large-scale naturalistic datasets in English across different grammar formalisms: phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar. This study establishes a dual nature of Node Count: we conclude that it indexes two opposing forces—processing facilitation due to predictability in immediate regions and processing inhibition due to contextual semantic integration in spillover regions. We also demonstrate that Node Count has a unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction, since its facilitatory effect explains reading time variance beyond that captured by a Transformer-based language model. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

articles.title: Estimating first impression accuracy and accuracy awareness among laypeople and scientific experts
articles.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Christoph Schild; Alex Lee Jones; Liam Satchell
articles.abstract: First impressions can influence various consequential decisions, yet their accuracy remains poorly understood due to mixed evidence, difficulties in integrating results across heterogeneous study designs, and widespread methodological limitations. Here, we present a large-scale, registered test of first impression accuracy. We created new stimulus database of 214 Dutch adults whose scores on various trait measures will serve as our accuracy criteria. Perceivers (n ≈ 550 Dutch adults) will provide approximately 175,000 judgments of ten commonly studied traits (HEXACO personality dimensions, intelligence, trustworthiness, dominance, and social status) based on five information types (neutral and smiling facial photographs, full-body photographs, audio and video clips). Next to estimating first impression accuracy across different traits and information sources, we will examine how well perceivers can predict their own first impression accuracy, and how well first impression researchers’ (n ≈ 222) beliefs about accuracy map onto the accuracy rates observed in our study.

articles.title: Beyond Universality: Do All Adolescent Minds Benefit from Mindfulness?
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Pawel Holas; Dorota Kobylinska
articles.abstract: Despite the rapid global implementation of school-based mindfulness trainings (SBMTs), empirical findings regarding their effectiveness in children and adolescents remain inconsistent. Large-scale trials and recent meta-analyses have challenged early optimism, raising critical questions about for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms SBMTs may be beneficial. This paper provides a synthesis of key factors, grounded in both theory and practice, that may help explain why mindfulness interventions vary in their effectiveness for adolescents. Based on existing research and insights from implementing SBMTs in school settings, we examine four interrelated domains: (1) curriculum characteristics, with particular attention to the role of embodied, mind–body practices and practice dosage; (2) the contribution of teachers, including personal mindfulness practice, embodiment, and relational engagement; (3) developmental considerations related to age, metacognitive capacity, and ethical challenges in assessment; and (4) contextual influences at the level of the school ecosystem and broader sociocultural environment. We argue that assuming universal effectiveness can overlook important sources of variability and may help explain the null or even negative outcomes reported in some studies. By reframing SBMTs as context-sensitive, developmentally attuned, and relationally embedded practices, this paper advances a conceptual framework to guide future research, intervention design, and implementation in educational settings.

articles.title: For Whom Do School-Based Mindfulness Programs Work? The Role of Personality in Adolescent Intervention Outcomes
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Dorota Kobylinska; Julian Mituniewicz; Szymon Szumiał; Pawel Holas
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives
School-based mindfulness programs (SBMPs) are increasingly implemented to support adolescent mental health, yet evidence for their effectiveness remains mixed. Recent research suggests that average effects may obscure meaningful variability in outcomes across individuals. The present study aimed to examine both the overall effectiveness of a 6-week SBMP and the role of personality traits in predicting individual differences in intervention outcomes. 
Method
This quasi-experimental study included 122 adolescents aged 12–14 years from 14 school classes, assigned to either an intervention group or a wait-list control group. Outcomes were assessed at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up, including anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties, well-being, mindfulness, psychological distress, and self-compassion. Personality traits (neuroticism, extraversion, and openness) were examined as predictors of differential response to the intervention using latent class growth analysis and logistic regression. 
Results 
At the group level, the SBMP did not produce significant effects across the examined outcomes compared to the control condition. However, person-centered analyses revealed meaningful heterogeneity in response patterns. Adolescents characterized by higher neuroticism and lower extraversion were more likely to show improvements across multiple domains, including reduced anxiety and psychological distress and increased well-being and mindfulness. Additionally, lower openness predicted improvement in psychological distress. These findings suggest that intervention effects were not uniform but concentrated among adolescents with greater baseline vulnerability.
Conclusions 
These results indicate that the effectiveness of SBMPs may depend less on average effects and more on individual differences in responsiveness. Mindfulness training may be particularly beneficial for adolescents with specific personality profiles associated with higher psychological vulnerability. These results highlight the importance of moving beyond universal approaches toward more targeted implementation of mindfulness-based programs in school settings. 
Keywords: mindfulness, adolescence, personality, training, SBMPs

articles.title: Verifying verification strategies of quantifiers using Bayesian cognitive modeling and eye-tracking: A Registered Report
articles.authors: Canaan Tsabary; Weike Huang; Shiru zhang; Tamar Johnson; Jakub Szymanik; Ingmar Visser; Alexandra Sarafoglou
articles.abstract: The quantifiers most and more than half, despite often being held to be truth-conditionally equivalent, display diverging representations and behaviors. This has led researchers to hypothesize differing ‘verification strategies’, whereby more than half is evaluated by a more precise, explicit, rule-based process than most. To date, however, the case for this has been built exclusively on behavioral results, offering limited insights into the potential mechanism. Our study will combine eye-tracking with a Bayesian hierarchical cognitive model (Sarafoglou et al. 2026), providing a psychophysiologically informed and computationally explicit investigation of verification strategies. Native Dutch speakers will evaluate 228 quantifier statements, including ‘de meeste’ (most) and ‘meer dan de helft’ (more than half), using dot-array stimuli varying in visual complexity (‘few’ vs ‘many dots’), to test the credibility of divergent verification strategies. We conducted a pilot study (n=9) to refine the experimental design. We predict increased vagueness (α), meaning threshold (β), and response noise (γ) for most in the Bayesian cognitive model, in line with previous behavioral findings; as well as larger saccades for most, and greater pupil constriction for more than half (especially under the ‘many dots’ condition), reflecting differences in visual search strategy and attentional breadth. Our results indicated that there was XXX evidence [supporting/against] the hypothesis that the three parameters were greater for most in the Bayesian cognitive model (BFrc = XXX). There was XXX evidence [supporting/against] the hypothesis that saccade amplitudes were larger for most (BF+c = XXX). Pupil constriction was increased for XXX, indicating XXX evidence [in favour of/against] our hypothesis (BF+c = XXX). Finally, there was XXX evidence [supporting/against] an interaction between dot count and quantifier on pupil size, such that the 'many dots' condition resulted in a greater decrease in pupil size for XXX compared to XXX (BF+c = XXX). These results [offer credibility to/offer mixed evidence for/challenge] the hypothesis that more than half is associated with a more precise, ‘counting to a criterion’ verification strategy.

articles.title: Do Mindful Partners Make a Difference? A Meta-Analytic Test of the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model in Romantic Couples
articles.authors: Sin U Lam; William T. Hoyt; Caroline M. Swords; Siyan Gao; Alaina Srivastav; Simon Goldberg
articles.abstract: Objectives: Mindfulness is consistently linked with individual well-being and relationship functioning, yet it remains unclear systemically whether mindfulness reliably “crosses over” within romantic couples — such that one partner’s mindfulness is associated with other partner’s outcomes after accounting for dyadic interdependence. We conducted a model-testing meta-analysis (MTMA) based on the Actor–Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) to estimate actor (self-self), partner (self-partner), and interdependence (partner similarity) effects of mindfulness on couples’ relationship outcomes. Methods: We searched six databases (PsycINFO, PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Trials) for quantitative dyadic studies linking one partner’s mindfulness to the other partner’s outcomes across relational domains. Thirty-seven independent studies (12,396 couples) met inclusion criteria. We conducted a multivariate meta-analysis to estimate APIM-implied correlations (r*) and derived path coefficients, with 95% CIs from 1,000 bootstrap samples. Results: Cross-partner correlations were small but significant (rs* = .16 and .16 for male-to-female and female-to-male associations, respectively). However, corresponding APIM partner effects were close to zero and nonsignificant (βs = –.01), indicating no reliable crossover. Actor effects were significant (βs =.22 and .21 for male and female partners, respectively). Interdependence effects were also significant for partners’ mindfulness (r* = .27) and outcomes (r* = .42), indicating meaningful within-couple covariation. Discussion: Findings suggest that mindfulness is reliably associated with individuals’ own relationship functioning and shared dyadic processes, but not with a robust direct partner effect. These results indicated that partner associations may reflect shared couple-level influences rather than direct crossover, highlighting the implications of dyadic modeling and couple-level interventions.

articles.title: Youth Irritability in Context: Real-Time Within-Person Associations with Inhibitory Control
articles.authors: Yotam Aroch; Roni Partouche; Noa Oded; Reut Naim
articles.abstract: Background: Irritability, defined as proneness to anger, is widely prevalent among youth and is associated with significant psychosocial impairment. Inhibitory control, a key self-regulatory process, has been conceptualized as a central factor associated with irritability, although empirical findings remain limited and mixed. Yet, the daily-life manifestations of both irritability and inhibitory control remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied predominantly on single-session laboratory paradigms that are context-independent and cannot capture fluctuations in these constructs as they unfold in daily life. To address these limitations, the current study used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to examine how real-time, momentary inhibitory control relates to youth irritability in daily life. Methods: Using a dual-informant framework, 71 youth and their parents (youth: M = 13.22, SD = 2.21; 57.75% female; parents: 90.15% female) completed a 7-day EMA protocol administered twice daily, alongside a daily youth inhibitory control performance via a mobile version of the Stop-signal Task (SST). Results: Multilevel modeling (MLM) of prompt-level data indicated that momentary increases in youth irritability, characterized by real-time anger, frustration, and anger response to unmet expectations, were robustly associated with concurrent inhibitory control difficulties across both youth and parent EMA reports (βs > 0.07, adjusted ps < .042). Specifically, elevated irritability was associated with greater impulsivity and increased difficulty stopping actions when asked. However, irritability was not associated with behavioral inhibitory control performance derived from the mobile-SST. Conclusions: Findings suggest that youth irritability is a dynamic, context-sensitive state associated with momentary fluctuations in perceived inhibitory control difficulties in daily life. The lack of association with mobile-SST suggests that EMA-based reports capture real-world regulatory difficulties not fully reflected in behavioral task measures. These results underscore the value of momentary assessment approaches for identifying high-risk windows of irritability and regulatory vulnerability, with implications for developing precise, just-in-time interventions.

articles.title: Self-Promotive Interdependence: Cultural Models of Success in Sub-Saharan Africa and Beyond
articles.authors: Annabella Osei-Tutu; Erin Wang; Cristina Salvador; Amber Gayle Thalmayer; Keiko Ishii; Luzelle Naude; Tong Suo; Elizabeth Shino; Amelie Rossmaier; STEPHEN ASATSA
articles.abstract: In many social contexts, group success is perceived as crucially dependent on members’ personal achievements, as in team sports. We propose that this form of interdependence—centered on a shared model of how group success is realized through individuals’ striving and achievement, termed self-promotive interdependence—is particularly pronounced in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). We examine whether this culturally shared model manifests in the balanced activation of positive socially disengaging emotions (e.g., pride) and positive socially engaging emotions (e.g., connection) upon success, regardless of whether the success is personal or belongs to an ingroup member. To assess the distinctiveness of self-promotive interdependence, we tested participants in five cultural regions: SSA (N = 3,638), the Middle East (N = 401), Latin America (N = 570), Japan (N = 592), and the United States (U.S., N = 812). We found that a relatively pronounced pride-connection balance in both self-success and an ingroup member’s success—a signature of self-promotive interdependence—was most consistently observed in SSA. Notably, the regional patterns differed systematically: pride–connection balance emerged primarily for self-success in Japan, primarily for ingroup-success in the Middle East, and for neither in Latin America and the U.S. These findings provide the first large-scale cross-cultural evidence for self-promotive interdependence in SSA. Moreover, they suggest how cultural regions may differ in the models of success through which personal achievement and collective outcomes are linked.

articles.title: (Not) Replicating the effects of iconicity in lexical decision task: a study in Brazilian Portuguese
articles.authors: Mahayana Cristina Godoy; Thayná Cristina Ananias; David Michael Sidhu
articles.abstract: Iconic words are characterized by a sense of resemblance between their form and their meaning. The most common examples are onomatopoeias such as “cock-a-doodle-doo” or “woof-woof,” but recent research shows that speakers of various languages perceive a relationship between sound and meaning in various words of their language. This is the case for English words such as crunchy, zigzag or wiggle, whose sonority is perceived as mapping onto their meaning (Winter et al., 2023). Recently, psycholinguistic research has investigated whether iconicity influence language processing. Sidhu, Vigliocco and Pexman (2020) ran a lexical decision task with words varying in their iconicity level. Their results show that the more iconic a word is, the quicker participants react to it, thus suggesting that iconicity may have a facilitatory effect in word recognition. We replicated their study with a sample of Brazilian Portuguese speakers and Brazilian Portuguese words to test their main claim that reaction times in a classic lexical decision task could be influenced by the stimuli’s level of iconicity in a neurotypical population of adults. Our results showed no facilitatory effect of iconicity in reaction times or accuracy, suggesting that the findings of the original study do not necessarily replicate to all other languages. We review differences between English and Brazilian Portuguese that may account for the divergence in results across the two languages. Stage 1 protocol for the current study was published on 02/24/2026 and can be accessed in < https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/v4hy7_v1>.

articles.title: Factor Structure and Symptom Profiles of the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS): A Meta-Analytic Mean and Covariance Structure Analysis
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Johanna Einsiedler; Timo Gnambs
articles.abstract: The Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) is one of the most widely used clinician-rated instruments for assessing depressive symptom severity, particularly in pharmacological intervention studies. Despite its widespread use, evidence on the dimensional structure of the MADRS remains inconsistent. In this Registered Report, we propose a meta-analytic mean and covariance structure analysis of the MADRS to examine (a) which latent structure best represents MADRS responses and how reliably its factors are measured, (b) whether items or symptom dimensions function differently across clinical (diagnostic group, pharmacological treatment, assessment time point within treatment) and measurement-related (language version) moderators, and (c) whether diagnostic groups, pharmacological treatment regimens, and treatment stages are associated with distinct latent symptom profiles.

articles.title: Interpreting Neuropsychological Test Discrepancies: An Error-Adjusted Approach
articles.authors: Paul Skirrow; Christine Canty; Sarah Kember
articles.abstract:
Introduction:
Differences between neuropsychological test scores are often interpreted using simple thresholds based on standard deviation units. Although widely used, these approaches do not explicitly account for measurement error and may lead clinicians to infer the presence of deficits where none exist.
Method:
This paper describes an error-adjusted approach in which observed differences are evaluated relative to the expected measurement error of the tests involved. Drawing on classical test theory and methods already used within existing test batteries, the standard error of the difference is derived from the standard errors of measurement of the two tests. The size of the observed discrepancy is then expressed relative to the size of the shared error.
Results:
The resulting error-adjusted difference (EAD) provides an index of the size of a discrepancy relative to measurement error. A worked example illustrates how interpretation of the same difference varies as a function of test reliability.
Conclusions:
The method is intended as a practical complement to existing approaches, particularly in contexts where normative or regression-based comparisons are not readily available.

articles.title: Etic and Emic Models of Musical Preference in Brazil
articles.authors: Frederico Gonçalves Pedrosa; Verônica Mgalhães Rosário; Mariana Freitas Bahia dos Santos; Carlos Eduardo Pimentel
articles.abstract: The MUSIC model provides a robust etic framework for musical preferences, but its universal applicability may overlook cultural nuances. This study examined the adequacy of the MUSIC model in Brazil and developed a combined etic-emic alternative – the RITMO model – to assess comparative fit and predictive power for functional outcomes. A sample of 457 adults completed measures of musical preferences (STOMP-R and EPM-Z), coping through music listening (CML), affect (PANAS), and quality of life (WHOQOL-bref). Structural diagnostics revealed that the etic MUSIC model collapsed into extreme multicollinearity (VIF > 270.0) in the Brazilian context, indicating significant construct bias. Conversely, the RITMO model demonstrated a healthy orthogonal structure and superior model fit (lower AIC/BIC) across all functional outcomes when compared to MUSIC. Hierarchical analyses confirmed the RITMO model's incremental validity, quadrupling the explained variance for Negative Affect and identifying meaningful associations for Avoidance Coping where the etic framework was virtually blind. Specifically, Movimento emerged as a primary predictor of Negative Affect and Avoidance Coping, suggesting mood-congruent processing, while Orgânico predicted Problem-focused Coping. These findings suggest that musical preferences in Brazil function as proximal resources for emotional regulation, highlighting the necessity of culturally grounded models to understand the functional utility of music.

articles.title: Processes of change in cognitive-behavioral psychotherapy for procrastination: moderation and longitudinal mediation analyses of randomized controlled trial data
articles.authors: Magdalena Pietruch; Joachim Kowalski; Weronika Maria Browarczyk; Jarosław M. Michałowski; Marek Wypych
articles.abstract:
Objective. Procrastination is a common self-regulatory difficulty leading to impaired well-being. Although cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is considered the most promising intervention for procrastination, it remains unclear whether outcomes vary across individuals and which mechanisms drive therapeutic change. To address these gaps, we synthesized key mechanistic accounts of procrastination in an integrative cognitive-behavioral (ICB-P) model outlining processes involved in development and persistence of procrastination. We then comprehensively examined the processes of change in CBT for procrastination.
Methods. Candidate moderators and mechanisms of therapeutic change were examined in secondary analyses of pooled data (N = 459) from two randomized controlled trials comparing CBT for academic procrastination with a wait-list control. Procrastination severity and a wide set of candidate mechanisms were assessed at pre-, mid-, and post-intervention. Moderation analyses and longitudinal structural equation models with contemporaneous (within-wave) and lagged (cross-wave) mediation paths were applied.
Results. Participants with greater baseline emotion regulation difficulties benefited more from the intervention, whereas dysfunctional beliefs associated with some cluster B personality disorders were linked to lower improvements. Baseline depression, anxiety, or ADHD symptoms did not moderate outcomes. Regarding mechanisms of change, increased task value and proactive control mediated both contemporaneous and lagged reductions in procrastination. Contemporaneous effects were mediated through increased positive and decreased negative task-related affect, improved perseverance, emotional clarity, and internal attributions of success.
Conclusions. Findings suggest broad applicability of CBT for procrastination. Optimized interventions could enhance the implicated mechanisms, i.e. target task-related affect and self-regulation, or incorporate additional components. Directions for future research are discussed.

articles.title: Integrating Social Determinants in Brain Health Research: A Framework and Toolkit
articles.authors: Laurence Kirmayer; David Benrimoh; Tasmia Hai; Maxime Montembeault; Jai Shah; Stefanie A Tremblay; Vivian Welch
articles.abstract:
Despite growing recognition that social and environmental factors profoundly shape brain
development and function, systematic approaches for incorporating social determinants of health
(SDH) in neuroscience research remain limited. This paper provides a framework for SDH
integration in brain health research, organized in two parts. Part I examines conceptual
foundations: we review the concept and history of SDH, the reasons SDH matter for neuroscience,
and offer a critical comparative analysis of seven major SDH frameworks (WHO/CSDH, PHAC,
PROGRESS-Plus, ADRC SSDoH, PhenX, NINDS, and Kirkbride et al.) alongside the cultural-
ecosocial (CES) framework that serves as the paper’s integrative architecture. Part II addresses
implementation: we present a measurement toolkit organized around core SDH domains with
validated instruments and Canadian-specific resources including the SPARK tool and CIMD;
methodological guidance across the full research life cycle from community-engaged study design
through multilevel and systems-based analysis; a tiered ethics framework; and a best-practices
summary table. Particular attention is given to the Canadian research context.

articles.title: Introducing the One-Shot Download Task: Testing the validity of a new and simple measure of online pro-environmental behavior
articles.authors: Daniel Farrelly; Tia Lippitt; Harvey Thompson
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Measures of actual pro-environmental behaviour are increasingly in environmental psychology due to their increased ecological validity over self-report measures. Here we introduce a new such measure, the One-Shot Download Task (OSD), a brief online behavioural measure in which participants choose between incurring personal costs (completing a tedious task) or environmental costs (downloading unnecessary files associated with carbon emissions). Two studies were conducted (Study 1: N = 104; Study 2: N = 96) that assessed the OSD’s criterion validity by examining associations with measures of eco-anxiety, environmentally minded consumer behaviour and environmental attitudes, while Study 2 also tested whether social influence in the form of exposure to “watching eyes” stimuli increased pro-environmental choices in the task. It was found that OSD scores positively correlated with environmentally minded consumer behaviour and the Preservation dimension of environmental attitudes, but not with eco-anxiety or Utilization attitudes. Furthermore, participants exposed to watching eyes selected significantly more environmentally friendly options (higher scores on the OSD). These findings provide initial evidence for the validity of the OSD as a measure of actual pro-environmental behaviour, demonstrating expected relationships with established environmental constructs and sensitivity to social influence. Given its simplicity, low cost, and accessibility, the OSD offers a practical addition to the growing range of behavioural measures available to environmental psychological researchers, although further validation is warranted.

articles.title: Seeing the Self in Memory: Visual Perspective and the Remembered Self
articles.authors: Peggy L. St. Jacques
articles.abstract: Autobiographical memory both reflects and reshapes the self. In this chapter, I argue that visual perspective, the vantage point from which events are mentally viewed, is a core representational process through which remembering situates the self in space and time. The chapter synthesizes behavioural, phenomenological, neural, and philosophical work showing that own-eyes and observer-like perspectives differentially modulate vividness, emotion, and narrative content, and flexibly relocate the self within reconstructed scenes. I review evidence that posterior parietal regions, particularly angular gyrus and precuneus, translate retrieval goals into embodied simulations that support perspective shifts. Building on theories of experiential and temporally extended selves, I propose that perspective structures relations between remembering and remembered selves and tracks transformations of memory with objective and subjective time. Treating visual perspective as a dynamic retrieval orientation clarifies how autobiographical memory can simultaneously preserve continuity and enable change, providing a mechanism by which identity is maintained, revised, and regulated across the lifespan.

articles.title: Directed Recognizability in AI-Biographical Conversational Agents: Design and Evaluation in the Digital Afterlife Context
articles.authors: Dennis Riccardo; Thomas Keller; Mirella Moser
articles.abstract: Generative AI enables digital legacy systems that transform personal data into interactive conversational agents. Yet authenticity in such systems remains underspecified, especially from the perspective of living Data Donors whose data are used to construct the agent. This paper introduces directed recognizability as a design and evaluation lens for AI-biographical conversational agents. We present an AI Biographer that guides users through a structured biographical interview, generates a personalized agent, and supports post-interaction self-recognition evaluation. In an exploratory mixed-methods study with 15 participants, agents’ directed recognizability were evaluated positively overall. Value coherence and situational response patterns were recognized most reliably, while emotional resonance and humor congruence were more fragile. The findings suggest that authenticity should not be treated as complete replication, but as a bounded, interactional form of recognizability grounded in salient values, communicative patterns, and biographical context.

articles.title: Why Risk it, When You Can {rix} it: A Tutorial for Computational Reproducibility Focused on Simulation Studies
articles.authors: Felipe Fontana Vieira; Jason Geller; Bruno Rodrigues
articles.abstract: Computational reproducibility remains limited in psychological research, despite widespread norms for sharing data and analysis code. One reason is that reproducibility exists on a continuum, ranging from partial transparency—such as providing scripts or software version numbers—to fully executable research compendia that regenerate all results from raw code. In this article, we introduce Nix and the {rix} R package as a practical framework for achieving full computational reproducibility in simulation-based research. We provide a step-by-step tutorial demonstrating how {rix} can be used to define, build, and share isolated, project-specific software environments that precisely capture R versions, package dependencies, system libraries, and integrated development environments. We further illustrate this workflow by reproducing a complete manuscript using Quarto and the {apaquarto} extension, showing how analyses, figures, and text can be regenerated in a single, executable pipeline. Together, these tools lower the technical barrier to robust, end-to-end reproducibility and offer a scalable solution for simulation studies and methodological research in psychology and related fields.

articles.title: Trait cognitive and somatic anxiety differentially impact recognition in visual working memory binding tasks
articles.authors: David Spalding; Marc Obonsawin; Louise A. Brown Nicholls
articles.abstract: A series of visual feature binding experiments were conducted to assess effects of trait cognitive and somatic anxiety on attention and working memory. Experiments 1 and 2 assessed participants’ recall of sequentially presented colour-shape combinations. In Experiment 1 the role of executive attention in binding was assessed via task instructions to encourage participants’ direction of attention toward specific memory items. In Experiment 2, the role of perceptual distraction in binding was assessed via presentation of a to-be-ignored visual suffix. No effects of anxiety were observed in either case. Experiments 3 and 4 assessed single-probe recognition at different memory loads (3 or 4 items). In Experiment 3, binding was compared with feature recognition. Trait cognitive anxiety was associated with improved feature memory, while trait somatic anxiety was associated with reduced binding memory. In Experiment 4, the effect of cognitive load on binding was assessed (number repetition vs backwards counting). Participants reporting moderate and high trait somatic anxiety demonstrated reduced binding recognition, compared with those reporting low anxiety. Results suggest that trait somatic anxiety limits binding recognition, but trait cognitive anxiety may aid feature recognition. Somatic anxiety may therefore be a more sensitive indicator of cognitive deficits than cognitive anxiety, at least regarding visual working memory, reflecting the different attentional focus associated with trait anxious apprehension and arousal. This helps to clarify the effect of the subjective experience of anxiety on attention and visual working memory.

articles.title: Sensory Discomfort Across the Migraine Cycle
articles.authors: Sarah M Haigh; Melissa Cortez; Rory Thompson; Anastasia Chevychalova; Janea Santiago; KC Brennan
articles.abstract: Sensory discomfort is a core complaint in migraine, particularly during the migraine headache, and fluctuates over the migraine cycle. Here, we examine the potential for monitoring sensory discomfort as a predictive symptom of approaching migraine pain. Two studies were conducted. For Study 1, we assessed sensory sensitivities using standardized self-report questionnaires across multiple sensory modalities to identify the sensory domains where individuals with migraine (with and without aura; tested during a non-headache phase) exhibit greater discomfort than headache-free individuals. We found that individuals with migraine reported greater discomfort in visual, odor, and tactile modalities interictally compared to headache-free individuals, but not in the auditory modality or in their susceptibility to motion sickness. Study 2 was a prospective daily diary study, lasting 30 days; here, we asked a group of individuals with migraine (with and without aura) to report on their sensory discomfort using modified (for daily use) versions of the same questionnaires used in Study 1. While we found that sensory discomfort was maximal during the day of migraine pain, we also found that discomfort increased the day prior to the head pain in visual (for migraine with aura only) and in auditory modalities (for both migraine with and without aura). This highlights the utility of tracking sensory discomfort to predict approaching migraine pain but emphasizes the need for an individualized approach to ascertain which sensory modality best reflect the migraine cycle for the individual. This approach also provides insight into the changes in underlying neural mechanisms of migraine.

articles.title: Racial-Ethnic and Gender Inequities in School SEND and Youth Justice Responses to Children and Young People's Mental Health: Population-based Cohort Study using Linked Administrative Data in England
articles.authors: Sorcha Ní Chobhthaigh
articles.abstract:
Background:  Mental health difficulties increase risk of justice system contacts, and justice involvement increases risk of and exacerbates existing mental health difficulties. However, discrimination influences both whether children’s needs are supported and the likelihood of justice system contacts. Examining patterning in Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND) provision for Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs and youth justice contacts may identify escalation pathways and opportunities for equitable support.
Methods: In partnership with young people and community stakeholders, we analysed population-level linked school and police administrative data for 3.7m children (born 1997-2003) who attended state schools in England. We examined rates, timing and risk ratios for the sequencing of SEND-for-SEMH and youth justice contacts.
Results: Children ever recorded with SEND-for-SEMH had markedly elevated rates of youth justice contact, and vice versa. First justice contacts clustered between ages 14-16, though Black Caribbean, Mixed White-Black Caribbean, Romani, and Irish Traveller boys experienced steeper increases from age 12. Most racially and ethnically minoritised boys, alongside Romani and Irish Traveller girls, were significantly more likely than White British boys to have youth justice contacts before/without SEND-for-SEMH. Following SEND-for-SEMH, racially and ethnically minoritised boys and Irish Traveller girls were at greater risk of contacts.
Conclusions: Findings reveal intersectional discrimination in criminalisation of children and shed light on the complex bi-directional relationship between identified mental health need and youth justice contacts. A healing-centred, public health, multi-agency approach is urgently required to break the vicious cycle between unmet mental health need and youth justice system contacts.

articles.title: Using Generative AI to Foster Student Sense of Belonging in Mathematics
articles.authors: Kole Andreas Norberg; April Murphy; Logan De Ley; Ethan Shafran Moltz; Husni Almoubayyed; Steve Ritter
articles.abstract:
We developed the A.I. Math Personalization Tool (AMPT) to enhance cultural relevance in math word problems by giving students agency over the content. AMPT leverages generative AI to directly engage students as co-authors of math word problems. Through scaffolded conversations, the AI allows students to provide the context for a problem. Then, the AI integrates that context with the pedagogical standards of a target learning domain. We measured the attitudes of students to-
wards mathematics before and after interaction with AMPT. After a single 30-minute session co-authoring math word problems with AMPT, students’ sense of belonging in mathematics significantly increased, while other attitudes remained unchanged. AMPT provided students with the opportunity to express themselves and see their interests reflected in the math domain. After experiencing this level of agency over math content, their sense of belonging in mathematics increased. The results of this
study demonstrate the potential for generative AI to enhance student choice, motivation, and, ultimately, achievement in mathematics.

articles.title: Incomplete compensation without further adaptation: A large-sample acoustic analysis of bite block speech in masking noise
articles.authors: Timothy Kevin Murphy; Hung-Shao Cheng; Caroline A Niziolek; Benjamin Parrell
articles.abstract: The speech system maintains intelligibility even when articulatory movements are restricted. Researchers often study this compensatory mechanism using a bite block to constrain jaw movement. While early reports indicated that speakers fully negate bite block effects on vowel acoustics, more recent reports found only partial compensation, suggesting the potential for continual adjustments. We investigated a large sample (n=55) of speakers who performed a bite block task while their auditory feedback was masked. We found incomplete immediate compensation and no adjustments over time, suggesting that continual compensation for bite block effects on vowel acoustics requires auditory feedback.

articles.title: The Living SEB Skills Project: A Living Resource for Review and Meta-Analysis of Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Skills
articles.authors: Tommaso Feraco; Margherita Calderan; Gerardo Pellegrino
articles.abstract: The social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills framework was recently proposed as an integrative model for soft skills/socio-emotional competencies, clarifying their definition and distinction from personality traits. To support open and cumulative research in this area, we introduce the Living SEB Skills Project, a continuously updated database combining ongoing literature searches, an open repository of coded studies and effect sizes, and an interactive application enabling customizable meta-analyses. Using meta-analyses of correlations and meta-analytic structural equation models, we demonstrate the database’s utility by testing the predictive and incremental validity of SEB skills for academic achievement on the current available data (364 publications, of which 30 met the criteria for the living review and 19 [26 samples] for the quantitative synthesis). The Living SEB Skills Project sets out as a transparent, dynamic and openly accessible tool to accelerate and ease cumulative science and synthesis within the SEB skills framework and beyond.

articles.title: Social Learning Undermines Performance and Increases Inequality When Decision Outcomes Depend on Prior Success
articles.authors: Paul K. Bergmann; Dominik Deffner
articles.abstract: Individuals often estimate the risks and benefits of decision alternatives from their own experiences and the behaviours and outcomes of others. In both simulations and experiments, social learning has largely been found to improve decision-making compared to individual learning alone. While previous work treated decision outcomes over repeated choices as independent, in many real-life contexts, including financial investments, life-course developments, or social networks, decision outcomes depend on previous outcomes, producing self-reinforcing ``the-rich-get-richer" dynamics. The adaptive consequences of social learning under such dependent, multiplicative conditions remain unknown. Using social reinforcement learning models in an agent-based simulation framework, we identify diverging effects of several well-established social learning strategies. In contrast to independent, additive environments, nearly all forms of social learning in multiplicative environments undermined performance and increased inequality  compared to individual learning. This occurred because an overly risk-seeking but fortunate minority provided systematically misleading cues. Payoff-biased learning strategies, usually considered a safeguard against herding, further deteriorated decision-quality, whereas conformity-biased copying slightly improved performance. These findings were observed even under time-optimal utility transformations of private and social payoff information. Together, our findings demonstrate disadvantageous collective learning under stochastic multiplicative growth, emphasizing that nearly all forms of social influence exacerbate inequality in these systems.

articles.title: Fast reading and fast listening: Evidence for individual differences in sentence comprehension
articles.authors: Fabian Roman Eckert; Kyla McConnell
articles.abstract: Although individual differences have been documented throughout the language system, it remains unclear whether native speakers vary in the efficiency with which they process naturalistic sentences. In the current study, we capitalized on the fact that language comprehension is constrained by the rapid and transient nature of incoming input and used speed pressure to reveal individual differences in sentence comprehension that would otherwise be difficult to detect. Two hundred native English speakers completed speeded listening and speeded reading tasks in which temporal pressure was systematically increased and comprehension was assessed using semantic plausibility judgments. Performance showed substantial individual differences in both tasks, and scores on the two tasks were highly correlated, suggesting a modality-independent source of variance in sentence comprehension efficiency. We also examined whether this variability was associated with domain-general processing speed, short-term memory, and print exposure. Domain-general processing speed was a strong predictor of performance in both tasks, suggesting that the speed of lower-level processing constrains successful sentence comprehension. Print exposure predicted performance in both reading and listening, consistent with the view that reading experience strengthens lexical representations in ways that benefit comprehension across modalities. Together, these findings indicate that temporal pressure can reveal meaningful variation in sentence-comprehension efficiency and suggest that native speakers differ not only in the linguistic knowledge they possess, but also in the efficiency with which that knowledge is deployed during online comprehension.

articles.title: On the relationship between pain and the sense of body ownership: a systematic review
articles.authors: Marco Lezcano; Francesca Santoni; Michele Scandola
articles.abstract: Human senses enable an individual to describe and set boundaries for themselves in relation to the outside world while creating their own body representation. Given the dynamic nature of such a complex structure, integrations of external elements inside the own body schema are possible. Since the 90s, scientific research has highlighted this phenomenon through the Rubber Hand Illusion (RHI) paradigm. Over the years, the literature on the induction of RHI has highlighted distinct, and often contradictory, effects on pain modulation, sometimes underscoring its analgesic, hyperalgesic, or null influence on pain sensation. Given RHI's role in therapeutic settings, the current systematic review seeks to shed light on its effects on pain perception and the role of pain in inducing RHI. Following the PRISMA guidelines, we retrieved and included 30 papers in our work. Overall, the evidence suggests that the relationship between body ownership and pain is context-dependent. When the embodied hand was presented as healthy and multisensory stimulation was congruent, RHI was more often associated with analgesic effects. Conversely, when the embodied hand appeared injured, threatening, or sensitised, embodiment tended to increase pain sensitivity or unpleasantness. Null findings were also common, suggesting that ownership induction alone is insufficient to reliably modulate pain. Studies using painful or nociceptive stimulation showed that RHI can be induced not only by innocuous touch. These findings suggest that pain and ownership interact through multisensory, affective, motivational, and predictive mechanisms. Future studies should use larger samples, clearer measures of ownership, and clinical populations.

articles.title: Emerging Stressors and Adolescent Depression and Anxiety: Associations and Cumulative Burden Among Kenyan Adolescents
articles.authors: Tom L Osborn; Natalie Nicolle Coon; Faith Kamau; Rosine Baseke; Wendy Mmbone Musonye; Christine Wasanga
articles.abstract: Depression and anxiety among young people are rising globally, and one proposed explanation is that the stressor environment of adolescence has changed. Emerging stressors—person-level exposures born of connectivity, technological change, and collective crises—are increasingly linked to adolescent distress in high-income countries; sub-Saharan Africa, where these exposures are spreading fastest, remains almost entirely unstudied. We examined whether emerging stressors across two domains—digital (problematic social-media use, online appearance comparison) and global (climate-change anxiety, pandemic-related stress, exposure to ethnic-political violence)—were associated with depression (PHQ-8) and anxiety (GAD-7) among Kenyan adolescents in two cross-sectional school studies (N = 5,592; Mage = 15.9 years; 49.8% female; 74 schools), and whether risk accumulated as stressors co-occurred; exploratory analyses tested body-esteem mediation and moderation by gender and structural disadvantage. After establishing scalar measurement invariance across samples, symptoms were regressed on each stressor within its study, using covariate-adjusted linear and logistic mixed-effects models with school random intercepts, estimated in 20 multiply imputed datasets with false-discovery-rate correction; we report standardized βs (per SD) and odds ratios for clinically elevated symptoms (≥ 10). Cumulative burden was the count of co-occurring stressors (top-tertile exposure). Clinically elevated depression (28.1%) and anxiety (24.5%) were common and did not differ between samples. Every stressor was independently associated with both outcomes (βs = 0.20–0.36; odds ratios = 1.39–1.92 per SD), with climate-change anxiety strongest (βs = 0.33–0.36). The odds of clinically elevated symptoms roughly doubled with each additional co-occurring stressor (odds ratios = 1.86–2.32), monotonically, in both samples. Indirect effects through body esteem were significant but small (0.04–0.09) relative to direct paths (~0.30), and associations were not moderated by gender, socioeconomic status, or family structure. Emerging stressors are consistently associated with adolescent depression and anxiety in Kenya, and their burden accumulates as exposures co-occur. Future studies should test longitudinal associations and all stressor domains.

articles.title: Semantic Interference in Blocked-Cyclic Word Production with Different Stimulus Types, Tasks, and Response Modalities
articles.authors: Stefan Wöhner; Andreas Widmann; Sophia Forchner; Erich Schröger; Jörg D. Jescheniak
articles.abstract: Blocked-cyclic picture naming is a prominent tool in word production research. It was found that responses were slower when the stimuli were presented blocked by semantic category than when they are presented intermixed. Wöhner et al. (2021) extended the task to sound naming and found that the semantic interference was much larger in sound naming (e.g., a barking) than in picture naming (e.g., of a dog), by a factor of approximately three, even when the same words were produced (e.g., “dog”). We explored possible reasons for this differential interference pattern. We replicated the differential interference when the stimuli were presented briefly, ruling out that it results from substantial overlap between stimulus processing on the one hand and phonological response preparation and pre-articulatory self-monitoring on the other. In contrast, we found similar-sized interference when the sounds and pictures were replaced with spoken and written words to which participants responded with the translation in their second language, ruling out that the differential interference results from different input modalities. We also observed the differential interference in sound and picture naming when the spoken response was replaced with a typed response, ruling out that it results from a specific (spoken) response modality. Overall, the data demonstrate the robustness of the differential interference in sound and picture naming and provide evidence that the semantic interference in blocked-cyclic naming is effectively shaped by early stimulus-specific perceptual and semantic – “lead-in” – processes, which precede lexical selection. These early processes require more attention in word production research.

articles.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles.title: Putting Attentional Control to a Normative Test
articles.authors: Dominik Grätz; Kerstin Fröber; Ulrich Mayr
articles.abstract: Attentional control deficits are often invoked to explain individual or aging-related differences in how people allocate attention. Yet what constitutes optimal attentional allocation, and how closely human behavior approximates it, remains poorly understood without a normative analysis of the allocation space.  We introduce a novel incentive-compatible attentional allocation paradigm that is amenable to normative analysis. On each trial, participants either maximize piece-rate earnings by focusing on a primary task or, at an opportunity cost to earnings, check cues indicating which of two primary tasks is currently rewarded. Normative modeling of value/allocation functions revealed wide variability in optimal strategies across decision contexts, but also relatively flat utility surfaces, implying weak normative constraints. Empirically, participants were less sensitive to most decision variables than the model predicted while showing pronounced individual and aging-related differences (Experiment 1). However, the opportunity cost of orienting, relative to the baseline response rate, emerged as a key normative determinant of allocation differences across individuals and age groups. Indeed, individual and age differences were largely explained by variations in relative orienting costs: because older adults were slower on the primary task but not in cue checking per se, their effective cue-checking costs were smaller, leading to more frequent cue use. In preregistered Experiments 2–4, we confirmed the causal nature of the effects of relative orienting costs. We argue that a normative framework clarifies when attentional differences reflect adaptive, cost-sensitive optimization rather than control deficits, and outline testable implications for further research on how people allocate attention.

articles.title: Willful Ignorance in the Context of Antibiotic Prescribing
articles.authors: Alina Schneider; Miroslav Sirota; Rian Gross; Lars Korn; D. Elisabeth C. Sievert; Cornelia Betsch; Robert Böhm
articles.abstract: Healthcare professionals tend to overprescribe antibiotics despite knowing the risks of antibiotic resistance. This tendency, amplified under diagnostic uncertainty and patient pressure, suggests that mechanisms beyond lack of risk awareness or knowledge sustain overprescription. One such mechanism may be willful ignorance—deliberately avoiding information about the consequences of one’s prescribing decisions. By allowing healthcare professionals to justify immediate antibiotic prescriptions that prioritize short-term self-interests over long-term collective benefits, willful ignorance may contribute to persistent overprescribing. Despite its practical relevance, this psychological mechanism has not yet been empirically investigated in the context of antibiotic prescribing. To test this empirically, we conducted a preregistered online experiment with healthcare professionals (N = 698) from the United States and the United Kingdom. Participants completed an adapted version of the Moral Wiggle Room Task, a behavioral decision-making paradigm designed to investigate willful ignorance. This task compares choices across a full information condition with low diagnostic uncertainty, and a hidden information condition with high diagnostic uncertainty that can be voluntarily reduced. The results support the presence of willful ignorance in antibiotic prescribing. Healthcare professionals were more likely to prescribe antibiotics immediately in the hidden vs. full information condition. Even healthcare professionals who voluntarily reduced diagnostic uncertainty prescribed more antibiotics immediately than those who received diagnostic information involuntarily. These results highlight the role of willful ignorance in antibiotic prescribing and suggest practical implications for policymaking, such as promoting transparent environments to guide appropriate antibiotic prescription choices.

articles.title: No Evidence for the Affective Expectation Model: Replication of Geers and Lassiter (2003)
articles.authors: Lukas Röseler; Christopher Albert Doetsch; Nico Förster; Ann-Kathrin Bruzsa; Marie Deublein; Eva-Monika Rieger; Charlotte Schmidt; Amelie Seitz; Antonia Wild; Desirée Gianella
articles.abstract: According to the Affective Expectation Model (AEM), people’s evaluations of experiences depend on their expectations. This generally happens in an assimilative way (positive expectations lead to positive experiences) unless there is a strong discrepancy between the expectation and the experience. In this case, a contrast effect occurs (positive expectations lead to negative experiences). We conducted an online replication of Study 1 from Geers and Lassiter (2003) where affective experiences were positively correlated with affective expectations for people with a low need for cognition and negatively correlated for people with a high need for cognition. None of the original effects could be replicated, that is, affective experiences did not differ between the groups and were not moderated by need for cognition. We discuss potential limitations of the AEM. The study’s preregistration, data, and materials are available online (https://osf.io/rge23/).

articles.title: Uptake and adherence to prophylactic antibiotics and vaccination during meningitis outbreaks: a rapid review to inform incident response
articles.authors: Lauren S Ross; Alex F. Martin; Eleanor M Jackson; Charlotte Hall; Freya Mills; Poppy Ellis Logan; Holly Carter; Carla Hobart; Richard Amlôt; James Rubin
articles.abstract:
Background: Meningitis outbreaks require the rapid implementation of prophylaxis to limit transmission and reduce severe health outcomes. Evidence from similar outbreaks indicates that uptake (i.e. initiation of) and adherence to (i.e. completion of) prophylaxis can vary substantially, with implications for outbreak control. 

Aim: To synthesise evidence on uptake of, and adherence to, prophylactic antibiotics and vaccination during meningitis outbreaks globally and the factors associated with these health behaviours. 

Method: This rapid review was pre-registered (https://osf.io/mwdch). Searches were conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycInfo, and Web of Science on 01 April 2026. PRISMA and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines and NICE recommendations for risk of bias assessment were followed. Data were extracted on study context and population, outbreak characteristics, and rates and factors associated with uptake and adherence. 

Results: Of 8,370 records screened, 21 studies were included. Reported rates of uptake and adherence differed widely between studies. Studies consistently identified higher uptake among younger people, women/females (vs men/males), and those with higher socioeconomic status. Social and structural factors, particularly education settings, parental influence, and trust in healthcare providers affected behaviours. No patterns were observed by serotype. Evidence on adherence, particularly for antibiotics, was limited. 

Conclusion: The consistent finding of higher uptake in younger groups contrasts with other outbreak contexts and highlights the importance of risk perception during outbreaks. During meningitis outbreaks, older people and those who consider themselves at low risk are less likely to follow prophylaxis regimes. Accessible delivery and risk-based communication may help address this.

articles.title: Kia Tīmata Pai Video Project: Impact of an oral language intervention (ENRICH) on linguistic aspects of educator-toddler interactions
articles.authors: Yuxin Zhang; Tugce Bakir-Demir; Mele Taumoepeau; Karen Salmon; Elaine Reese
articles.abstract: This study investigated the impact of an educator-implemented oral language intervention, Enhancing Rich Interactions (ENRICH), on linguistic aspects of educator-toddler interactions. Twenty-four early childhood classrooms were assigned to either ENRICH or an Active Control condition; ENRICH educators received professional development in serve-and-return interactions. For book-reading, results revealed effects of ENRICH for educators' shorter conversational turn length and children's increased utterances over time. An exploratory analysis further showed a more balanced child-to-educator conversational turn ratio during book-reading in ENRICH centers. However, there were no significant effects of ENRICH for linguistic aspects of educator-toddler interactions in mealtime, play, group, and diapering/toileting contexts. Professional development programs aimed at improving educator-toddler interactions should consider focusing on specific contexts where the intervention shows promise, alongside strengthening components targeting speech quality across daily routines.

articles.title: Inter-individual similarities in internal models predict similarities in the perception and neural processing of scenes
articles.authors: Micha Engeser; Daniel Kaiser
articles.abstract: Every individual person perceives the visual world in their own unique way, yet we still know little about the origins of these individual differences. Here, we propose that idiosyncrasies in internal models—mental representations of what the world should look like—shape how individuals perceive and process natural scenes. To characterize these internal models, participants drew what they considered the most typical version of a given scene category. Using a combination of deep learning tools, we quantified inter-subject similarities in these drawings and used them to predict inter-subject similarities in perceptual task performances and neural responses to a fully independent set of natural scenes. Individuals with more similar internal models showed more similar scene categorization performance and judged several scene properties (typicality, usability, and complexity) more similarly. Moreover, variations in participants' internal models predicted inter-subject correlations in BOLD time courses in the lateral occipital and lateral prefrontal cortices. These results provide a novel, mechanistic explanation of how perceptual and neural alignment across individuals is shaped by idiosyncrasies in prior experience.

articles.title: Dual-process theory and decision-making in large language models
articles.authors: Oliver Brady; Paul Nulty; LIli Zhang; Tomas Ward; David McGovern
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making scenarios, altering how people make choices. Despite the seemingly ‘superhuman’ capabilities of LLMs in some domains, there are pitfalls in the decision-making performance of LLMs and they should therefore be used with caution. In this Review, we examine LLM outputs through the lens of dual-process theory and against the backdrop of human decision-making.
