articles.abstract: How individuals think about stress—their appraisals and beliefs—directly shape stress responses. This meta-analysis assessed the efficacy of psychological interventions aimed at helping people value stress as growth supportive and use it to thrive, referred to as stress optimization interventions, on physiological (cardiovascular and neuroendocrine) and subjective stress-related outcomes. Data from 35 studies (total N = 6,834) that used randomized designs and reported biological or self-reported outcomes before and after stress reappraisal, stress mindsets or a combination of these interventions were analyzed. Random-effect models indicated that stress optimization interventions functioned to increase cardiac output (CO; d = 0.41), decrease total peripheral resistance (TPR; d = 0.47), and reduce salivary cortisol levels (d = 0.20) in acute stress contexts, with small-to-medium effect sizes. These effects were accompanied by small-to-high heterogeneity as a function of outcome (I² from 0% to 67%). No effects of interventions on pre-ejection period (PEP; d = 0.11) or heart rate (HR; d = -0.03) emerged. For subjective outcomes, interventions showed small but reliable benefits. Stress optimization interventions reduced recent distress (d = 0.30) and improved affective responses (d = 0.15), with meaningful heterogeneity across both. In contrast, interventions exhibit no significant effect on reported stress arousal (d = 0.07) with little heterogeneity. Collectively, findings demonstrate that stress optimization interventions can help improve physiological and subjective stress-related responses in acute stress settings, offering a promising approach to promoting resilience, thriving, and performance when navigating everyday social stressors.

articles.title: People make history-dependent decisions in Markovian environments
articles.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Evan Russek; Ionatan Kuperwajs; Nitzan Shahar; Marcelo G Mattar; Wei Ji Ma; Tom Griffiths
articles.abstract: Many real-world decisions are history-dependent, such that the appropriate action depends on recent events. However, people may also encounter history-independent environments, where all information relevant for action selection is contained in the current state. Here, we tested whether people can adapt to such environments by analyzing the behavior of 74,304 online chess players, focusing on 183,775 instances where a player encountered the same board position in two different games. In chess, the configuration of pieces on the board fully specifies the information relevant for optimal play, making the history of the current game redundant. Nevertheless, we find that players’ behavior is biased to be history-dependent. Our findings challenge assumptions about humans’ ability to decide based on a task’s abstract state representation, instead suggesting that contextual traces play a significant role in biasing behavior even when individuals are highly trained and motivated to perform at their best.

articles.title: The Value of Self-Deception: How Conflict in Action Selection May Shape Human Beliefs and Behavior
articles.authors: Boaz Rosenberg; Eran Eldar
articles.abstract:
Human decision-making often involves conflict between different processes involved in guiding behavior. Here we develop a formal account of how self-deception could arise as a byproduct of such conflict. The core idea is that when a process’s preferred action is rejected due to conflict with competing processes, it may still influence choices by promoting attentional biases that shift decisions toward its preferred action. 
We use three proof-of-principle simulations to derive the consequences of this architecture. The simulations show that, under specified conditions, agents can learn to value attentional bias, maintain uncertainty when it makes bias effective, and devalue bias when it is unsustainable. We then outline the qualitative predictions of the model for human behavior, including biased belief formation, self-handicapping, procrastination, and depressive and bipolar-like conditions. We conclude by comparing these predictions with those of existing theories and discussing implications for psychological research and clinical practice. 
This framework offers new theoretical insights into the adaptive and maladaptive functions of self-deception, suggesting it as a key organizing construct for understanding a range of everyday and pathological human behaviors.

articles.title: The Youth-GEMs project: genetic and environmental interactions underlying trajectories of youth mental health
articles.authors: Bart Ruttens; Sinan Guloksuz; Bochao Lin; Covadonga M. Díaz-Caneja; Elisabeth Binder; Jonathan Mill; ESMERALDA RUIZ; Karim Lekadir; Maria Bulgheroni; Jim van Os
articles.abstract: Most mental disorders emerge before age 24, yet the mechanisms shaping youth mental health trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Youth-GEMs consortium performing a multidisciplinary, multisite research project funded by a European Union Horizon-Staying-Healthy-2021 grant. The Youth-GEMs project (Gene Environment interactions in Mental health trajectorieS of Youth) has an integrated, developmental framework that examines how genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors dynamically interact to influence risk and resilience across adolescence and young adulthood. The project combines developmental (epi)genomic mapping of the human brain, genomic analyses of trans-syndromal phenotypes, exposome-wide environmental assessment, and Artificial Intelligence-based modelling to identify predictive and actionable markers of mental health trajectories of young people. By harmonizing multimodal data from existing population-based cohorts and by establishing the first international, trans-syndromal clinical cohort of help-seeking young people, Youth-GEMs is generating biologically informed polygenic and exposomic scores, cell-type-specific regulatory annotations, and interpretable machine-learning models. Continuous engagement with young people, clinicians, and stakeholders ensures that findings translate into tools for early detection, monitoring, and personalized intervention. Together, these efforts aim to advance mechanistic understandings of youth mental health, improve prediction of emerging illness, and support the development of evidence-based, developmentally sensitive approaches to prevention and care.

articles.title: When ASMR Becomes Unpleasant: Acoustic Features and Visual Context Shape Emotional Responses to Eating Sounds
articles.authors: Daigo Hozaki; Hibiki Okita; Takahiro Ezaki; Hirohito M Kondo
articles.abstract: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos can evoke both pleasant and unpleasant emotional responses. Eating sounds appear to produce especially large individual differences in these experiences. We examined how acoustic features and visual context shape emotional responses during eating-sound ASMR. Ninety-six participants were randomly assigned to one of four stimulus-presentation conditions: auditory-only (Aud), audiovisual congruent (AV-C), audiovisual incongruent (AV-I), or visual-only (Vis). Participants were presented with eight 30-s ASMR clips (4 min total) and provided continuous ratings of their emotional responses on a 3-point valence scale: unpleasant, neutral, and pleasant. Emotional responses differed across conditions. The Aud condition elicited the most unpleasant ratings. This negative bias was reduced when visual information accompanied the sounds, especially in the AV-C condition. Response-category distributions showed the same pattern. To identify low-level acoustic features associated with moment-to-moment changes in emotional responses, we extracted four acoustic features: amplitude, spectral centroid, spectral bandwidth, and instantaneous roughness. For each feature, we computed across-ear averages and left–right differences. We computed lagged Spearman cross-correlations between acoustic features and emotional responses. In the Aud condition, increases in across-ear average amplitude and roughness were followed by shifts toward more unpleasant responses. Evidence for comparable acoustic–emotion coupling was limited in the AV-C condition. These findings suggest that emotional responses to eating-sound ASMR are shaped by acoustic features and visual context. Congruent visual information may reduce unpleasant responses by clarifying the sound source and changing how eating sounds are interpreted.

articles.title: Falling on Fertile Ground: National Identity Rhetoric Mobilises Those High in National Narcissism
articles.authors: Chiara Zazzarino; Stefan Leach; Aleksandra Cislak; Magdalena Formanowicz; Jan Nikadon; Aleksandra Cichocka
articles.abstract: Politicians frequently talk about national identity and commitment to national interests. We examined whether such rhetoric mobilises supporters by exploring the role of national narcissism—a belief that one’s nation is exceptional and entitled to special treatment. We tested whether national identity rhetoric boosts the audience’s national narcissism or whether it appeals to those already high in national narcissism. In six experiments, conducted in the US and UK (Ntotal = 3,716), we measured reactions to AI-generated political speeches (Studies 1, 3, 4 and 6) and social media posts (Studies 2 and 5). We found that participants high in national narcissism perceived messages promoting national identity as more persuasive and were more willing to share them on social media, compared to messages rejecting national identity (Studies 1 and 2) or neutral ones (Studies 3 and 4). We also found that national narcissism predicted voting for (Studies 1 and 3), and broadly supporting (Studies 4 and 6), leaders who appealed to national identity in their speeches, compared to those who did not. In Study 5, we corroborated our findings by relying on behavioural indices of engagement with social media posts on a mock platform. Similar effects were observed for messages promoting national identification and national narcissism. Furthermore, in Study 6, national narcissism predicted support for leaders promoting (vs. rejecting) national narcissism regardless of their partisan affiliation (as Republican vs. Democrat). Across the six studies, we found no reliable evidence that national identity messages affected participants’ own national sentiments.

articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely heavily on gaze to provide and receive information in social settings. Gaze indicates where another person is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. This scoping review synthesises 352 peer-reviewed articles addressing gaze as a meaningful cue in social situations. The term gaze semantics refers to the systematic ways in which gaze carries, shapes, modifies, or constrains meaning. The evidence suggests that gaze typically does not encode determinate mental content: One gaze pattern can carry different meanings across settings. We organise the empirical literature around four operations of gaze. Gaze orients by directing attention toward something, addresses by making someone socially implicated, qualifies states, traits, and other social cues by modifying how they are interpreted, and coordinates by shaping what becomes relevant next in interaction. These operations can act in parallel and are not tied to specific gaze characteristics. One gaze pattern can perform several operations simultaneously, and each operation can be realised by different gaze patterns. Gaze interpretation is inferential and depends on signal properties, perceptual and interactional availability, multimodal and sequential embedding, social and activity frames, gazer and observer states, and interactional history. We conclude that gaze constrains social interpretation while typically remaining semantically underdetermined.

articles.title: Reciprocal Relations Between Motivational Factors and Error Reactions:  A Cross-Lagged Panel Study in Primary School Children
articles.authors: Cara-Sophie Enste; Jana Spear; Carolin Burmeister; Markus Dresel; Robert Grassinger
articles.abstract: Constructive learning environments inevitably confront students with errors, making adaptive reactions to errors a central component of effective self-regulated learning. Although theoretical models posit motivational beliefs as key antecedents of adaptive error reactions, their reciprocal development over time, especially in primary school, remains largely unexplored. The present longitudinal study investigated within-person autoregressive and cross-lagged relations between two motivational factors (academic self-concept, subjective task value) and two types of adaptive error reactions (affective-motivational, action-related) across three measurement points spanning 1.5 years in third and fourth grade students (N = 494). Using two-level cross-lagged panel models, we found substantial autoregressive stability for all constructs, with motivational beliefs showing higher stability than error reactions. Academic self-concept predicted subsequent affective-motivational reactions to errors, but not vice versa, suggesting a primarily unidirectional developmental pathway. Subjective task value showed reciprocal relations with both affective-motivational and action-related error reactions: valuing a task more predicted more adaptive reactions to errors, while engaging in adaptive error responses predicted later increases in subjective task value. Notably, action-related reactions to errors exhibited stronger reciprocal effects than affective-motivational reactions, indicating that effortful error correction may enhance perceived task value. Together, findings show that primary school students adjust subjective task value more readily than academic self-concept in reaction to error experiences. These results refine the existing model of learning from errors by demonstrating bidirectional links between motivational factors and error processing and underscore the importance of fostering subjective task value as well as academic self-concept to support adaptive reactions to errors in early schooling.

articles.title: A modifiable tunnel environment to study experience of space (TEnvi)
articles.authors: Mark Wünsche; Mathis Jording; Ralph Weidner; Kai Vogeley
articles.abstract:
Perception of spatial extent depends on multiple sources of information, including geometric and motion-related cues such as perspective and optic flow, as well as oculomotor signals (e.g., vergence), yet experimental control over these factors is often limited. We introduce TEnvi, a stimulus-generation framework that enables systematic manipulation of geometric parameters of a tunnel-like virtual environment under continuous optic flow.
TEnvi allows independent manipulation of tunnel width, height, and depth while maintaining controlled perspective projection, shading gradients, and distance-dependent luminance attenuation. The framework integrates an interactive graphical interface with a reproducible rendering pipeline supporting both real-time preview and batch stimulus export. Camera motion is defined as a function of time, ensuring consistent optic flow across preview and rendered stimuli and preventing cumulative numerical drift.
To demonstrate the utility of the stimulus framework, a behavioural validation experiment was conducted in which participants rated perceived room size while the geometric dimensions of tunnel width, height and depth were manipulated relative to a baseline configuration. Ratings were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model with manipulation type and manipulation level as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept. Manipulations of tunnel width produced graded increases in perceived room size across levels. Manipulations of height produced small shifts relative to baseline but did not differ reliably across levels, while manipulations of tunnel depth showed no detectable influence on perceived room size. These results illustrate how the stimulus framework can isolate the perceptual contribution of geometric parameters and provides plausible data of size perception grounded in tunnel width manipulation.

articles.title: Perceived Error Climate in the Classroom as an Important Aspect of Student Support: Interactions with Student Motivation?
articles.authors: Cara-Sophie Enste; Jana Spear; Carolin Burmeister; Markus Dresel; Robert Grassinger
articles.abstract: A positive perceived error climate as a form of student support and individual motivation (aca-demic self-concept, subjective task value) are linked to adaptive affective-motivational and action-related reactions to errors in secondary school students. However, research mostly over-looks primary education and lacks an interactive understanding of individual and contextual determinants: students with different motivational characteristics may require varying levels of support (i.e. error climate). Testing this, we conducted multilevel analyses across German and Maths with 997 third- and fourth-grade students from 78 classrooms. Both motivational factors, the individually perceived error climate and its aggregated classroom perceptions positively predicted adaptive reactions to errors. For adaptive affective-motivational reactions to errors, interactions emerged: the effect of error climate was especially pronounced for students with high academic self-concepts and students with low subjective task value. This indicates that constructive support while dealing adaptively with errors can reduce negative effects of unfavourable task value or enhance beneficial effects of high academic self-concepts.

articles.title: Momentary Cognitive and Self-Regulatory Predictors of Daily Alcohol Use: Intent vs. Inhibition
articles.authors: Jennie Lukoff; Ilse H. van de Groep; Reshmi Marhe; Willem-Paul Brinkman; Ingmar H.A. Franken; Andrew Jones; Joran Jongerling; Danielle Remmerswaal
articles.abstract:
Background. Drinking intentions consistently predict alcohol consumption, but findings for behavioral measures such as inhibitory control are mixed, particularly in earlier stages of use.
Methods. 142 recreational alcohol users (40 males, 102 females; M = 33.30 years, SD = 14.76) completed a four-day EMA study with three daily prompts assessing alcohol use, craving, perceived control, and planned use, directly followed by a mobile Go/No-Go task assessing inhibitory control. Bayesian multilevel models examined whether inhibition errors, planned use, craving, and perceived control predicted drinking at momentary and daily timescales.
Results. Momentary evidence indicated a positive association between planned use and drinking between (β = 0.18, 95% CrI [0.03, 0.31]) and within-persons (β = 0.31, 95% CrI [0.20, 0.42]), while negative within-person effects emerged for craving (β = -0.12, 95% CrI [-0.23, -0.02]) and perceived control (β = -0.41, 95% CrI [-0.52, -0.28]). Daily evidence found that planned use was positively associated with daily drinking (β = 0.84, 95% CrI [0.44, 1.24]), whereas perceived control was negatively associated with drinking (β = -0.78, 95% CrI [-1.21, -0.36]). No credible evidence was found for within-person effects on daily alcohol use.
Conclusions. Findings suggest that alcohol use in recreational drinkers, may be driven by intentions and self-regulatory beliefs, as opposed to momentary or daily lapses with inhibition. A negative within-person association between momentary craving and alcohol use, despite a positive linear study trend, may reflect a mismatch between the reference windows measuring craving (right now) and drinking (night before, last two hours).

articles.title: When ASMR Becomes Unpleasant: Acoustic Features and Visual Context Shape Emotional Responses to Eating Sounds
articles.authors: Daigo Hozaki; Hibiki Okita; Takahiro Ezaki; Hirohito M Kondo
articles.abstract: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos can evoke both pleasant and unpleasant emotional responses. Eating sounds appear to produce especially large individual differences in these experiences. We examined how acoustic features and visual context shape emotional responses during eating-sound ASMR. Ninety-six participants were randomly assigned to one of four stimulus-presentation conditions: auditory-only (Aud), audiovisual congruent (AV-C), audiovisual incongruent (AV-I), or visual-only (Vis). articles.title: Acute effects of competitive exercise context and competitive outcomes on mood responses
articles.authors: Sarah Reddin-Conroy; Carly Wender; Meabh Corr; Eric Magrum; Mika Manninen
articles.abstract:
Acute mood responses to exercise are recognised as important determinants of exercise
adherence, yet the influence of competitive team-game context on these responses remains
underexplored. This study compared acute mood responses between team-game and non-
competitive group exercise while controlling for exercise intensity. A randomised crossover
design was employed with 69 physical education students (age range = 19–30 years; 27
females). Participants completed two 20-minute sessions: an indoor soccer game (TS) and a
video-led group exercise session (GE). Mood was assessed pre- and post-exercise using the
Profile of Mood States–Short Form (POMS–SF), and intensity was measured using Borg’s
Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE). Data were analysed using linear mixed-effects
ANCOVA models. Both conditions produced significant and comparable reductions in Total
Mood Disturbance (TMD). However, the TS condition elicited significantly higher adjusted
post-session vigor compared to GE (Δ = 2.33, 95% CI [0.78, 3.88]), Benjamini-Hochberg
(BH) adjusted p = 0.024, d = 0.52). Within the TS condition, competitive outcome influenced
acute mood responses, with winners displaying less Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) (Δ = -
5.81, 95% CI [-11.24, -0.37], p = 0.037, d = 0.40) and Anger (Δ = -2.53, 95% CI [-4.23, -
0.83], adjusted p = 0.024, d = -0.77) compared to losers. These findings suggest that
psychosocial factors of team games – such as competition and cooperation – can contribute to
enhanced energy beyond the effects of exercise alone. Additionally, the findings imply that
even short recreational team games can lead to different mood responses between losers and
winners.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Individual Differences: A Perspective of the Differential Psychology, Personality Psychology, and Psychological Assessment Division of the German Psychological Society (DGPs)
articles.authors: Ramona Schoedel; Elisa Altgassen; Mitja D Back; Martje Buss; Markus Bühner; Julian M. Etzel; Benjamin Goecke; Sandra Grinschgl; Eric Grunenberg; Ole Hätscher
articles.abstract: In this paper, we examine artificial intelligence (AI) in the context of studying and measuring individual differences across three current topics: AI as a research tool, the design of human-AI interaction, and AI-assisted assessment. Drawing on selected examples, we illustrate the wide-ranging potentials of AI at the conceptual and methodological level, while also showing that its application raises new (research) questions - for instance regarding human competence in dealing with AI, the “personality” of AI systems, or psychometric standards in the use of AI-assisted assessment procedures. Against this backdrop, we discuss key prerequisites for a sustainable integration of AI into both research in personality psychology and individual differences, including critical validation, transparency, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the systematic consideration of individual differences in the responsible design of the human-AI interface.

articles.title: Revisiting the Interpretation of r and R2: A Comment on Funder & Ozer (2019)
articles.authors: Christian Thurn; Michael Dantlgraber
articles.abstract: The article by Funder and Ozer (2019) emphasizes the important aspect that small correlations can be relevant, both theoretically and practically. However, we contend on two key points: (1) We contend that, when choosing between r and R2 as measures of effect size, R2 remains the superior measure. (2) Furthermore, we argue that despite the justified criticism of traditional, rigid thresholds for interpreting effects, the newly proposed guidelines by Funder & Ozer (2019) carry a risk of overinterpretation by conflating two distinct dimensions: the magnitude of a correlation and the relevance of a correlation.

articles.title: Hallucination or confabulation? A psychological reinterpretation of erroneous outputs in large language models
articles.authors: Ignacio Rivero Covelo; Aryan H. Patel; Kaelan J. McDonough
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent but false outputs that are widely described as “hallucinations.” We argue that this term is psychologically imprecise. In clinical psychology and psychiatry, hallucinations are perceptual phenomena, whereas many erroneous LLM outputs are better characterized as constructive, plausibility-guided responses produced under insufficient informational constraint. We suggest that confabulation provides the more informative psychological analogue.

Drawing on work in psychopathology, memory, source monitoring, and natural language generation, we compare hallucinations, confabulations, and LLM errors as distinct classes of cognitive failure. Our central claim is that many LLM errors resemble confabulation more closely than hallucination because they involve coherent but false content generation rather than perception-like experience. This reframing revises terminology. Additionally, it clarifies the kind of process involved and connects AI discourse to established psychological theory. Finally, it generates testable predictions: such errors should increase under ambiguity, decrease with stronger external constraint, and remain schema-consistent rather than random. More broadly, the paper illustrates how psychological concepts can be used productively in interpreting artificial systems, while also showing the importance of distinguishing among superficially similar forms of error.

articles.title: How Will I Know If You Really Like Me? Assessing the Role of Appearance, Behavior, and Reciprocity for Meta-Liking Accuracy in Initial Social Encounters
articles.authors: Jana Bruns; Eva Bleckmann; Lisa Maria Niemeyer; Mitja D Back; Steffen Nestler
articles.abstract: In first social encounters, people regularly try to figure out whether others like them. When accurate, these meta-liking judgments enable individuals to more optimally engage in social interactions. Although previous research shows that people do know how much others like them, little is known about the processes leading to accurate meta-liking judgments. In the present, pre-registered research, we aimed to close this gap by investigating the role of a meta-perceiver’s appearance and behavior, others’ behavior towards that meta-perceiver, and the reciprocity heuristic in forming accurate meta-liking judgments. To this end, we used data from a round-robin study, in which N = 144 participants (Mage = 22.91, 67.6% female) took part in two group meetings, where they interacted with unacquainted others. After each participant had given a short self-introduction, participants indicated liking and meta-liking for each other participant. Additionally, trained raters judged participants’ appearance and behavior during the self-introduction. Results showed that people were able to correctly infer how much others generally liked them but hardly knew how much specific other liked them. Lens model analyses revealed that although one’s appearance and behavior were valid cues for being generally liked, meta-perceivers did not utilize most of these observable cues to inform their meta-liking judgments. However, the assumed reciprocity mediated both individual and dyadic meta-liking accuracy. In light of these findings, we discuss the role of self-observed behavior and stable personality characteristics as well as situational and motivational factors, presenting an integrative theoretical framework to explain generalized and dyadic meta-liking accuracy.

articles.title: The format of metaphorical meaning: Neurophysiological evidence for dynamic and flexible image-based representations
articles.authors: Federico Frau; Rosario Tomasello; Maddalena Bressler; Chiara Pompei; Fabrizio Luciani; Paolo Canal; Valentina Bambini
articles.abstract: Theories of metaphor comprehension have long debated the representational format of metaphorical meaning. While classical accounts describe metaphors as abstract propositional representations, other theories have, to varying degrees, argued that metaphor evokes mental imagery. Yet neurophysiological evidence that speakers construct mental images reflecting the complete figurative interpretation remains scarce. Here, we investigated whether metaphors give rise to mental images resembling those generated during imagery or whether they rely predominantly on propositional representations. We designed a novel picture-matching paradigm in which identical target pictures were preceded by either matching or mismatching stimuli across four tasks: another picture (Physical task), an adjective prompting imagery (Imagery task), a literal sentence (Literal task), or a metaphorical sentence (Metaphorical task). Across multiple levels of analysis of the EEG signal, the Metaphorical task patterned more closely with imagery than with literal language. Metaphors elicited enhanced P300 and attenuated N200 responses, greater recruitment of occipito-temporal visual regions, and stronger upper-alpha/lower-beta desynchronization than literal descriptions, indicating that participants constructed perceptually richer representations. These effects were further modulated by individual differences in imagery and vocabulary. However, at later stages, metaphors also diverged from imagery, which showed more pronounced brain signatures associated with memory retrieval and representational maintenance. These findings indicate that metaphorical meanings yield image-based representations while remaining constrained by propositional content. Collectively, the results confirm that metaphor “sets things before the eyes”, but it does so through the dynamic and flexible interaction of perceptual simulation with propositional information, in line with multiple representation theories of conceptual knowledge.

articles.title: Deviations in Distributions Perception through Imprecision and Accounting for Uncertainty through Abstract Representations
articles.authors: Nico Gradwohl; Benjamin Scheibehenne
articles.abstract: Perceiving the distributions of values we experience accurately is crucial for adaptive judgment and decision making. Previous research shows that people are quite adept at learning distribution information, so that many models of judgment and decision making assume that people accurately store it. However, a variety of deviations in distributions people report indicate that distributions are unlikely stored faithfully, even if the observed information is unbiased. To shed light on the origin of these deviations we review of literature on distribution perception and the cognitive processes underlying the encoding of numeric information. Based on this review, we outline a framework of three cognitive processing steps: perception and encoding, representation formation, and retrieval. Computational descriptions of these steps illustrate that deviations in previous work may originate from imprecise perception, retrieval, as well as integration into abstract representations that account for uncertainty. Based on predictions from the framework, we provide empirical results supporting that both imprecise perception and memory, as well as formation and storage of abstract representations contribute to deviations in the perception of distributions. Results also show that people unlikely just store information as precise instances that are retrieved to make judgments about distributions. This work contributes by connecting previously disconnected literature strands. It also shows that biases in judgments and decisions may not only be the result of biased processing of accurately stored distributions, but also of fundamental distortions in how values and their distributions are perceived.

articles.title: From Review to Synthesis: A Step-by-Step Methodological Guide to Systematic Reviews and Multilevel Meta- Analyses
articles.authors: Hu Meilan; Paye Shin Koh; Xun Ci Soh; Andree Hartanto; Nadyanna M. Majeed
articles.abstract: We provide a step-by-step guide on conducting a quantitative systematic review (i.e., meta-analysis) using the open-source programming language R, as well as conducting a multilevel meta-analysis, in contexts where effect sizes are non-independent (e.g., multiple effect studies from the same lab). Quantitative systematic reviews offer researchers a method to synthesise large bodies of literature, helping to clarify inconsistent findings, identify research gaps, and refine theoretical models. However, existing tutorials often assume prior knowledge and/or experience, often overlooking foundational concepts. To address this gap, a comprehensive walkthrough of the systematic review process is presented, covering pre-registration, literature search and retrieval, screening, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction following the PRISMA framework. We then present detailed guidance on how to conduct both traditional and multilevel meta-analyses in R. Specifically, the tutorial explains how to estimate overall meta-analytic effect sizes when effect sizes are independent (traditional meta-analysis) and when effect sizes are nested within labs (multilevel meta-analysis). Procedures for assessing heterogeneity, testing for publication bias, and conducting moderation analyses are also covered. To accompany this tutorial, we supplement annotated R scripts and R notebooks to support transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for researchers of all levels of experience.

articles.title: From Pathogens to Paintings: A Preliminary Investigation Into the Behavioral Immune System’s Influence on Visual Aesthetic Appreciation and Perception
articles.authors: Serkan Ozcakan; Mert Tekozel
articles.abstract:
As an antipathogenic psychological adaptation, the behavioral immune system has been associated with a broad spectrum of psychological phenomena, including mating, conformity, xenophobia, religiosity, social prejudice, and food preferences. Additionally, this system may influence artistic appreciation and perception. Activation of the behavioral immune system generally results in intolerance of morphological deviations, even toward stimuli that do not pose a real pathogen threat, as it operates on the “smoke detector principle.” Therefore, we hypothesized that participants exposed to pathogen threats would exhibit less appreciation for abstract paintings—those deviating significantly from figural reality—compared to those under other threats or nonthreat conditions. Supporting our hypotheses, participants under pathogen threat liked abstract and ambiguous paintings (those lying between realistic and abstract) less compared to those in the other two conditions. However, the prediction that ambiguous paintings would be perceived as more abstract under pathogen threat did not receive statistically significant support. These preliminary results suggest that psychology evolved in response to pathogen threats may also influence visual aesthetic appreciation.

Keywords: behavioral immune system, visual aesthetic liking, pathogen salience, art preferences, experimental aesthetic.

articles.title: The effectiveness of a therapeutically applied Dungeons and Dragons group intervention in a community mental health setting – Protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
articles.authors: Terry Rae; Matthew Modini; Poppy Watson
articles.abstract:
Objective 
The use of Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) in mental health treatment settings has grown in popularity and early efficacy investigations appear promising. However, the use of TA-RPGs for the treatment of anxiety and depression has rarely been studied in people who present with comorbid complex mental health issues. While one recent waitlist-controlled trial has reported that a TA-RPG (Dungeons and Dragons with embedded CBT) reduced mental health symptomatology, this now needs to be replicated with a more robust experimental design. Publishing this protocol methodology before the study is completed aims to increase transparency and aid other researchers conducting similar research in this advancing field.  
Methods 
The authors propose a two-group randomised controlled trial testing the efficacy of a CBT-infused, therapeutically applied, 8-week Dungeons and Dragons group program. An active control group will play board games for a comparable amount of time. Participants will be consumers receiving care at a community mental health centre with complex care needs. Outcome measures for anxiety and depressive symptomatology will be collected before and after participation in both groups, with the intervention group also completing outcome measures at 12 months follow up. In this protocol paper the intervention will be outlined in detail. The trial is registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12625000296437.

articles.title: Jurisprudential Drift in International Investment Law: From the Minimum Standard to Fair and Equitable Treatment
articles.authors: Barry Hashimoto; Kevin W. Gray; Kabir Duggal
articles.abstract: The meaning of the fair and equitable treatment standard in international investment law remains unsettled. One interpretation ties it to the customary minimum standard of treatment associated with Neer; another treats it as an autonomous and more demanding source of investor protection. States have repeatedly sought to tether FET to the minimum standard, most notably the United States, a principal architect of the investment regime and a major capital exporter. Yet arbitral jurisprudence has tended toward broader interpretations. This Article asks why. It argues that the shift cannot be explained by doctrine, state power, credible commitment, firm pressure, or arbitrator discretion alone. The better explanation is jurisprudential drift: interpretive movement produced within a specialized field of arbitrators, elite counsel, arbitral institutions, and commentators. Open-textured treaty language and arbitral autonomy create interpretive space; investor demand supplies background pressure for capacious protection; and legal counsel and arbitrators benefit, generally but unevenly, from a more complex and protective legal regime. Symbolic capital helps make some broader interpretations focal; reputational enforcement keeps arbitrators and counsel aligned with those interpretations; and secrecy, judicial economy, and peer review supply flexibility, allowing tribunals to manage difficult cases without turning exceptions into a new doctrinal baseline. The Article develops this theory, compares it with existing and reconstructed accounts from law, international political economy, and the social sciences, and evaluates it against the historical, doctrinal, and arbitral record surrounding the rise of the investment regime, the minimum standard, and FET. It concludes that the drift toward autonomous FET reflects a form of transnational legal authority generated through ordinary legal reasoning and coordination within the field of investment arbitration.

articles.title: Breaking Symmetry, Not Choosing Direction: A Model of Hierarchy as a Position Amplifier, and What It Can and Cannot Recover
articles.authors: Kristian Sestak
articles.abstract: Hierarchies form even among near-equals. Their inequality is usually read as meritocracy sorting on ability, as a coordination device a group needs, or as cumulative advantage in which leads compound. We give a falsifiable normal form for one further route, a symmetry-breaking amplifier of position. This is a multiplicative cascade that turns tiny, often capability-irrelevant differences into a large positional dispersion, Var(ln rho_eff) >> Var(ln k), where k is capability and rho_eff the density of favourable possibilities the environment makes accessible. On top of the normal form we draw the line the title names, between what such a hierarchy's trajectory can and cannot recover about its own origin. The dynamics (question A, whether the process amplifies or merely diffuses) are identifiable from a trajectory. We fix them with three results: a necessity theorem, a non-monotone dispersion-maximising gain that plain cumulative advantage does not produce, and a sqrt(tau) early-lead law that separates amplification from diffusion. Cumulative advantage is told apart not by the magnitude of early-lead persistence, which it can match, but by the non-monotone gain and by the collapse of that persistence under revocation. The seed (question B, whether what got inflated was capability or position, real skill or amplified noise) is not identifiable. We prove a non-identifiability theorem: the map depends on capability and position only through their sum, and it weights an early fluctuation almost like an inherited head start, so no statistic of the trajectory recovers the split. The informal statement that the amplifier keeps no signature of what it amplified is therefore a theorem rather than a metaphor, and it cannot be refuted by data. Identifying B requires an exogenous handle on capability that does not pass through the amplifier, such as quality fixed by construction, randomised, or a convergent later estimate. That handle returns not a verdict but a manufactured share, R = 1 - corr^2. We demonstrate the boundary on one large public dataset. A near-equal online-chess cohort whose order looks manufactured, in that it is decoupled from entry and locks in faster than diffusion, is found to be about 60% revealed skill (R approx 0.4) once a convergent skill estimate is admitted. The remaining behaviours of the model follow. Development requires the feedback, since at zero gain the process is a martingale, and the motion is non-ergodic, with the ensemble advancing while the typical trajectory peaks and declines. The contribution is not that hierarchy is noise. It is a precise account of what a hierarchy's own trajectory can, and cannot, tell us about where it came from.

articles.title: Who Appears, For What Purpose, and to Whom: Rethinking Deepfake Reception as Relational Configuration
articles.authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel
articles.abstract: Research on deepfake reception has expanded rapidly, yet its findings remain theoretically fragmented. Effects vary across genres, modalities, purposes, disclosure conditions, and receiver characteristics, while explanations often focus on isolated properties of synthetic artifacts or specific research traditions. This article argues that six structural biases—malignancy, stimulus, cognitive-declarative, universal receiver, modality, and narrative processing—have shaped not only what deepfake reception research has primarily examined, but also how the phenomenon itself has been conceptualized. To address this problem, the article proposes the Relational Deepfake Reception Framework (RDRF), which conceptualizes reception as emerging from the relationship between the depicted subject, the perceived purpose of the encounter, and the receiver, within a broader contextual envelope. Drawing on evidence across diverse empirical contexts, it further shows that findings often treated as inconsistent can be interpreted more coherently when viewed configurationally rather than through artifact-centered explanations. The framework generates testable propositions, identifies methodological implications for future research, and extends its relational logic to audio deepfakes. More broadly, it argues that explaining deepfake reception requires shifting the unit of analysis from the synthetic artifact to the relational encounter through which it acquires meaning.

articles.title: Information Management by Political Parties During the 2023 Gubernatorial Elections in Cross River State, Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Ekwo Gilbert Otu
articles.abstract:
This paper examines how political parties managed political information during the 2023 gubernatorial elections
in Cross River State, Nigeria. The objectives of the study were to examine the information management strategies
adopted by the All Progressives Congress (APC) and the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) and to assess the
effectiveness of these strategies in achieving electoral goals. Data were collected through survey instruments and
analysed using descriptive statistics and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) at the 0.05 level of significance. The
findings revealed that both the APC and PDP deployed multi-channel information strategies, including social media
campaigns, traditional media messaging, grassroots mobilisation, and data-driven targeting of specific voter blocs.
Although these strategies improved message speed, visibility, and engagement among some demographic groups,
their overall persuasive effect on undecided voters and their capacity to drive voter turnout were perceived as
moderate rather than strong. The ANOVA results further indicated no statistically significant difference between
the APC and PDP in the strategies adopted or in the perceived effectiveness of those strategies for achieving
electoral goals. The study concludes that while both parties have modernised their communication architectures,
the effectiveness of information management still depends on local networks, credibility, and the ability to bridge
the digital divide between urban and rural audiences. The study recommends that political parties should continue
to strengthen digital communication teams for rapid message dissemination while sustaining ward-level grassroots
structures and town-hall engagements, since face-to-face interaction remains essential for building trust, particularly
in rural communities and among older voters.

articles.title: Rethinking Poverty in Today's Developing World: A Reflexive Essay
articles.authors: Bui Thi Thao Trinh
articles.abstract: This reflexive essay explores the multifaceted nature of poverty in the contemporary developing world, moving beyond the traditional economic reductionism of the poverty line. Grounded in the context of post-Đổi Mới in Vietnam and the broader Southeast Asian region, the paper intertwines academic frameworks with personal narratives to challenge mainstream development discourses. Utilizing Jonathan Rigg's multidimensional typology, the essay critically examines four distinct faces of poverty: the residual poor lacking basic needs (Poverty 1.0), the unequal poor left behind by distributional gaps (Poverty 2.0), the produced poor marginalized by development processes such as dispossession, displacement, and casualization (Poverty 3.0), and the invisible unrecognized migrant workers (Poverty 4.0). By contrasting the lived experiences of the precariat, such as tech drivers working under heatwaves and informal workers, with the structural inequalities of market-led growth, the paper argues that modern poverty is continuously produced and reproduced by capitalist development processes. Finally, this essay highlights the necessity of a “wholeness of being” perspective, suggesting that addressing contemporary poverty requires not only economic growth, but inclusive policies, politicization, and a profound recognition of marginalized voices stemming from an empathetic understanding of reality from within.

articles.title: Already Living Inside It: A Reflexive Note on Development
articles.authors: Bui Thi Thao Trinh
articles.abstract: This reflexive note explores the contested and shifting understandings of development through lived experience in contemporary Vietnam. Moving through personal experiences - rural transformation in a farming village, urban inequality, work in a local social enterprise grounded in ecological values, and a visit to a K'ho ethnic minority community facing dispossession in the Central Highlands - the essay illustrates how the concept of development shifted: from modernity and economic growth, to human well-being, sustainable development, ethnodevelopment, and finally to something unresolved. Instead of arriving at an ultimate definition, the essay proposes that holding the question open, and being honest about its contradictions, is itself an intellectual and human commitment. Written before formal academic instruction began, this note documents what it looks like when theory meets a life that has already been living within it.

articles.title: The Grammar of Fear in Journalism
articles.authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel
articles.abstract: This study conceptualizes fear as both emotional grammar and an institutional regime that structure and constrain journalistic practice. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with Venezuelan journalists, it maps how fear is experienced across physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions to produce a refined typology of journalistic fears. Grounded in empirical evidence, it identifies five dynamic processes—anticipation, internalization, manifestation, management, and narrativization—through which fear permeates professional life and becomes routinized in news production. These processes generate an emotional grammar that organizes how fear is felt, expressed, and legitimized within journalistic culture, and an emotional regime through which such norms are institutionalized across individual, organizational, and societal levels. The resulting structure governs professional conduct, regulates the boundaries of speech, and shapes journalism’s role in society. The article advances a middle-range theory of communicative affect in journalism, offering a transferable framework for analyzing how emotions function as infrastructures of power and meaning.

articles.title: Ambivalent perception of “tojisha group” and tolerance of the group: Toward a sustainable space for cooperation among individuals to whom need belong and who possess the potential for agency
articles.authors: Takazumi Ono; Hiroko Costantini; Misato Nihei
articles.abstract:
Summary: In context emphasizing well-being of people with vulnerabilities and minority status, the term tojisha has gained widespread usage in Japan. The term tojisha refers to “an individual to whom needs belong and who possesses the potential for agency in relation to those needs,” and spaces designed for interaction among fellow tojisha are referred to as “tojisha groups” and such spaces are becoming increasingly common across various settings. While the importance of tojisha groups has been widely recognized, their potential negative aspects are rarely addressed. Therefore, we conducted an online questionnaire survey in two stages to examine the distribution of positive and negative perceptions of tojisha groups and to test the hypothesis that group tolerance is associated with these perceptions of the group. 

Findings: The results showed that many participants reported positive perceptions of tojisha groups. However, 40–60% also indicated negative perceptions, including feelings of not being able to understand each other or an inability to speak openly—even among fellow tojisha. K-means clustering identified four distinct clusters, including one cluster characterized by high scores on both positive and negative perceptions. In addition, group tolerance was associated with both positive and negative perceptions of the group. 

Applications: These findings suggest that while tojisha groups can offer meaningful and supportive experiences, they may also function as ambivalent spaces. Enhancing group-level tolerance may be crucial for ensuring that tojisha groups remain inclusive, supportive, and responsive to the diverse needs of their members.

articles.title: Equivocation and Erosion: How LLMs Undermine Catholic Religious Discourse
articles.authors: Jonathan Alan Karr; Matthew P. Lad; Demetrius Hernandez; Louisa Conwill; Walter Scheirer; Nitesh Chawla
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) offer opportunities for information dissemination, yet present challenges with upholding the distinct theological practices of the Catholic faith. By training on vast datasets, LLMs can generate responses that equivocate or blend together diverse perspectives. While this tendency can be beneficial for providing broad access to information, it can dilute the distinct theological tenets foundational to Catholicism. While these challenges may affect various faiths, we conduct a case study to investigate them within the Catholic tradition.

Unlike human religious authorities who may offer definitive interpretations based on Scripture, Tradition, and Magisterial teaching, LLMs present information in a flattened, generalized manner by smoothing over specific religious claims. This can weaken the emphasis on singular revelations or unique covenants. For instance, an LLM might present the concept of `God' in a way that blurs the distinct attributes of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as articulated in the Nicene Creed, into a generalized deity, thereby eroding particular theological distinctions.

Conversely, when prompted on matters of right or wrong within an ethical dilemma, an LLM might present a spectrum of opinions from secular frameworks. This can occur without distinguishing or prioritising the specific moral decrees found within Canon Law or the Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC). This synthesis of diverse ethical views, rather than a clear affirmation of distinct religious injunctions, exemplifies how LLMs can equivocate on matters of moral truth, potentially diluting authoritative guidance.

We examine how the outputs of general-purpose LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Llama, Gemini) and theological LLMs from differing religious traditions (e.g., Magisterium AI, Hyder.ai, RavChat) align with Catholic teaching. LLMs may inadvertently marginalize minority viewpoints within the Catholic Church or prioritise interpretations that align with cultural norms rather than traditional stances. Additionally, LLMs can shift interpretations in their outputs based on current events or political news. This can lead to a homogenization of religious discourse, obscuring the rich diversity and nuanced debates. However, when thoughtfully developed, these technologies can also provide valuable information that fosters understanding and encourages deeper engagement with religious texts and orthodox perspectives. In light of this, our study evaluates how LLMs align with the principles of Catholic Social Teaching, such as those found in the Rome Call for AI Ethics and Antiqua et nova. These frameworks underscore how technology should be used to foster human flourishing in alignment with divine wisdom while upholding religious truth.

articles.title: L'AUTONOMIE CONTEXTUELLE : VERS UNE THÉORIE NORMATIVE DE LA DÉLIBÉRATION CLINIQUE EN BIOÉTHIQUE
articles.authors: Hyacinthe Amour Gnahy
articles.abstract: L'autonomie constitue un principe fondamental de la bioéthique contemporaine, mais les modèles existants peinent à guider la décision médicale dans des contextes où interviennent simultanément le patient, les proches, les professionnels de santé et les contraintes institutionnelles. À partir d'une analyse philosophique comparative du principlisme, de l'autonomie relationnelle, des philosophies africaines de la personne et de l'éthique médicale confucéenne, cet article met en évidence l'absence d'un cadre normatif intégrateur de la délibération clinique. Il propose le concept d'autonomie contextuelle comme fondement d'une théorie normative articulant la volonté authentique du patient, les relations significatives, les déterminants contextuels et les responsabilités partagées. Structurée autour de cinq principes et illustrée par un cas clinique, cette approche offre un modèle de délibération permettant de légitimer les décisions médicales dans les sociétés pluralistes. L'autonomie contextuelle contribue ainsi au renouvellement de la bioéthique en proposant un cadre conceptuel conciliant exigences universelles et diversité des contextes de soin.

articles.title: Salvar la circunstancia en la era digital. Educación, información y democracia
articles.authors: K Ramos-Guasca; Liliam Alexandra Palomeque
articles.abstract:
Este trabajo examina el impacto del exceso de información en la sociedad contemporánea
y sus implicaciones para la educación y la democracia. A partir de casos como la
desinformación en redes sociales y de las limitaciones del llamado “mercado de ideas”,
se sostiene una tesis precisa, a saber, que el acceso masivo a datos no produce por sí
mismo ni pensamiento crítico ni un uso responsable del conocimiento, y que confundir
cantidad de información con calidad del juicio constituye un error de diagnóstico
con consecuencias políticas. En diálogo con Harari (2024), Floridi (2014), Piaget
(1970), Vygotsky (1979), Ortega y Gasset (2005), Arendt (1993) y Nussbaum (2010),
se argumenta que la formación técnica es condición necesaria pero insuficiente, y que
debe subordinarse a una educación orientada a fines éticos, políticos y cívicos. El
trabajo defiende que solo mediante marcos pedagógicos estructurales que articulen
alfabetización mediática, metacognición, diálogo crítico y virtudes democráticas es
posible enfrentar la aceleración informacional y evitar que la técnica se consolide como
instrumento acrítico. La propuesta articula un horizonte educativo capaz de resistir
la manipulación digital, fortalecer el juicio ciudadano y reorientar la técnica hacia la
construcción de sociedades más justas y democráticas

articles.title: Substitutes or Complements? Role Systems and Culture as Sources of Predictive Knowledge for Coordination
articles.authors: Lenard Strahringer
articles.abstract: When culturally diverse workers must coordinate, the prevailing design prescription is structural: make roles predictable and couple them tightly, so that workers can anticipate one another from the role system rather than from a common background. Implicit in this prescription is that structural and cultural sources of anticipation are interchangeable. I argue that the substitution holds only for routine coordination, because structure and culture supply predictive knowledge of different kinds: role systems generate scripted anticipation, which sustains routine exchange, whereas a shared cultural background generates communicative anticipation: the common ground partners need to renegotiate coordination in real time. I test this argument with passing data from professional European soccer. Across roughly five million directed dyad-match observations, shared official language predicts higher pass rates between teammates, but the advantage concentrates in dyads whose roles are behaviorally unpredictable and loosely coupled, precisely where structure offers little anticipatory support. For coordination flexibility, the pattern reverses: behavioral predictability does not moderate the cultural advantage, and tight role coupling amplifies it. Structural and cultural anticipation thus substitute for routine exchange but complement each other for flexible variation. Organizations that pair culturally diverse workforces with rigid structures may run efficiently on routine tasks while remaining poorly equipped to adapt.

articles.title: Seeing Yourself Deepfaked: The Experience of Synthetic Self-Confrontation
articles.authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel
articles.abstract: Deepfake research has focused on audience responses to synthetic representations of other people, with limited attention to the self as the synthetic subject. We introduce Synthetic Self-Confrontation (SSC) as a mediated self-encounter defined by the simultaneous experience of recognition and dissociation when one’s identity is artificially reproduced. Drawing on six focus groups (n = 32) in which participants evaluated deepfakes of others and were then shown non-malicious deepfakes of themselves, we identify four facets of SSC: a stable moral framework that shifts when participants become the subject; an intensity shaped by trust and experienced as curiosity or threat depending on creator; a hierarchy of identity markers in which the voice is more intimate and less detachable than the face; and an awareness of identity vulnerability that shifts concern from audience deception to self-directed false attribution. Synthetic media introduce not only epistemic but also ontological uncertainty in relation to the self.

articles.title: Reversing Brain Drain: An Econometric Framework For Regional Human Capital Retention
articles.authors: Emmanuel Kolade Adedokun
articles.abstract: This study investigates the structural determinants of regional youth out-migration and brain drain within South Korea, focusing on Gangwon Province as a critical case study. Utilizing regional empirical data spanning the 2015–2026 period, we construct a series of ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression models to isolate the impacts of regional employment opportunities, internal migration flows, healthcare quality of life indicators, and capital investment vectors on demographic retention. Grounded in Human Capital Theory (HCT), the empirical findings reveal that localized employment availability acts as a primary positive driver of youth retention, yielding a statistically significant coefficient of 1.142 (p = 0.004\). Conversely, acute healthcare infrastructure deficits and systemic out-migration vectors exert powerful inverse pressures that accelerate regional demographic contraction. Predictive analysis for the 2026–2030 horizon indicates that marginal nominal wage increases face diminishing returns due to the structural agglomeration gravity of the Seoul Metropolitan Area (SMA). The study concludes that mitigating regional human capital leakage requires provincial policies to pivot away from generalized physical infrastructure allocations toward targeted talent placement, localized industry-academic integration via the Regional Innovation System & Education (RISE) framework, and robust soft infrastructure enhancements.

articles.title: Breaking Symmetry, Not Choosing Direction: A Model of Hierarchy as a Position Amplifier, and What It Can and Cannot Recover
articles.authors: Kristian Sestak
articles.abstract:
Status hierarchies form even among people of near-equal ability. Their inequality is usually read as meritocracy (sorting by ability), as coordination (a group's need for someone to decide), or as cumulative advantage (small early leads compounding). This paper formalises a fourth possibility, often conflated with the third: hierarchy as a symmetry-breaking amplifier of position, a process that turns tiny, ability-irrelevant initial differences into large and durable gaps in standing. A population of near-equals sits at a symmetric state with no natural ranking; because that state is unstable, any noise, once amplified, breaks the symmetry and fixes an order by chance rather than by merit.
The mechanism is not new; the contribution is to make it precise and to tell it apart from its rivals, in three results. First, amplification is not just one route to inequality but a precondition for any durable, self-generated order: without the self-reinforcing feedback, early leads wash out. Second, the process is self-limiting, so concentration first rises and then falls with the strength of amplification, unlike ordinary cumulative advantage. Third, the model yields signatures that separate positional amplification from meritocracy, coordination, and cumulative advantage without measuring ability, using only how early the final order is fixed and whether an early lead survives when position can be contested and revoked. As amplification grows the winner decouples from genuine quality, the group advances while its typical member stalls, and a symmetric lower threshold makes an early loss as unrecoverable as an early lead is self-reinforcing. Illustrative evidence from an online cultural market, Wikipedia adminship, GitHub, and startup funding is reported as suggestive rather than confirmatory, and all results are reproducible from seeded simulations and public data.

articles.title: Introducing the Institutional Research Governance Familiarity Index (IRGFI): Development and Preliminary Validation
articles.authors: Seán Lacey
articles.abstract: Research Performing Organisations (RPOs) continue to strengthen institutional research governance in response to evolving expectations relating to research integrity, research ethics, open science, research security, responsible research assessment, and broader societal responsibilities. Despite considerable investment in governance frameworks, relatively little empirical attention has been given to whether researchers are familiar with the institutional governance instruments intended to support responsible research. This study introduces the Institutional Research Governance Familiarity Index (IRGFI), a practical, adaptable, and reproducible measure of researchers' familiarity with an RPO's formally approved research governance framework. The IRGFI was evaluated using data collected through two institution-wide surveys undertaken at Munster Technological University (Ireland) in 2024 (n = 252) and 2026 (n = 152). The index demonstrated good internal consistency across both survey administrations (Cronbach's α = 0.83 and 0.81), stable score distributions despite changes to the governance framework, and encouraging preliminary evidence supporting construct validity through expected associations with responsible research knowledge and institutional navigation (r = 0.29–0.50). Researchers' familiarity varied across governance instruments, while the proportion of respondents reporting familiarity with none of the listed governance instruments decreased from 14.3% in 2024 to 2.0% in 2026 (p < 0.001). The findings demonstrate that researchers' familiarity with institutional research governance can be measured using a practical, adaptable, and reproducible approach. The IRGFI provides RPOs with an evidence-informed approach to understanding how effectively institutional research governance reaches researchers and supports longitudinal monitoring of governance implementation and continuous institutional improvement.

articles.title: English-medium education and inequality in Saudi higher education: A scaffolded institutional model to reduce stratification
articles.authors: Rana Binsaeed; Samantha Curlw
articles.abstract: Universities have intensified their adoption of English Medium Instruction, but this growth has outpaced student linguistic preparedness and the institutional structures required to support it. Current implementation practices often overlook the cognitive and academic language demands placed on learners, resulting in a persistent misalignment between policy ambitions and classroom realities. This essay argues that a sustainable English Medium Instruction system requires a scaffolded, phased model that supports students’ academic language development alongside disciplinary learning. Viewed through a social inequality lense, rapid EMI roll out is associated with differential advantage for students from under resourced schooling backgrounds, lower income families, and those without access to private English capital, contributing to widening attainment and progression gaps. The essay proposes an integrated Scaffolding Unit as an equity-oriented institutional infrastructure that co-designs linguistically accessible tasks and assessments with content lecturers, and sequences support across years to prevent early academic exclusion. The model also flags an implementation risk. If scaffolding becomes a ‘premium’ resource available only to some programmes, it may reinforce a two-tier EMI system.

articles.title: Following the Feedback: Audience Engagement and Politicians’ Issue Attention on Social Media
articles.authors: August Lohse; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Snorre Ralund; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Political representatives increasingly communicate in social media environments where every message generates immediate and quantified audience feedback. Although likes, comments, and shares are not representative measures of public opinion, they provide visible signals about which issues attract attention from politicians' online audiences. We examine whether politicians subsequently devote more attention to issues that previously generated comparatively high engagement. Our analysis draws on 128,204 Facebook posts published by all 123 Facebook-active Danish Members of Parliament between 2011 and 2018. We find that issues receiving relatively more audience feedback are consistently more likely to appear in politicians' subsequent posts. This pattern is present across political topics and different forms of engagement, but weakens during election campaigns, when communication is likely to be more strategically constrained. The findings show how quantified platform feedback is systematically linked to the allocation of political attention and creates a distinctive form of communicative responsiveness to visible online audiences.

articles.title: Fostering Sustainable Undergraduate Research Ecosystems: A Self-Assessment Rubric for Institutional Planning
articles.authors: Adam I. Attwood
articles.abstract: This paper presents the Undergraduate Research Sustainability, Capacity, Access, Faculty Support, Faculty Facilitation, Operations, Learning, and Design Rubric (UR-SCAFFOLD), a self-assessment tool for examining the institutional conditions that make undergraduate research accessible, coordinated, and sustainable. The central claim is sociological: undergraduate research programs are not only pedagogical structures, but also organizational systems that distribute access, recognition, labor, authority, and opportunity. Drawing on studies addressing undergraduate research, mentoring, equity, institutional infrastructure, community engagement, and responsible technology use, UR-SCAFFOLD organizes program planning around seven dimensions: research pathways, mentoring capacity, operational infrastructure, digital and GenAI support, access and participation equity, evidence and sustainability, and visibility and mission alignment. Rather than proposing a universal model, the rubric offers a structured vocabulary for asking how students encounter research, how mentoring labor is supported, how administrative routines shape participation, and how opportunities are revised over time. The framework is intended for faculty, staff, program leaders, and administrators seeking to make the institutional work behind undergraduate research more visible, equitable, and durable.

articles.title: The missing Pacific influenza epidemics: Challenging where, when, and how the 1918–21 pandemic unfolded
articles.authors: Hampton Gaddy; Svenn-Erik Mamelund; Michael G Baker
articles.abstract: Influential accounts of the 1918 influenza pandemic report that many Indigenous Pacific populations escaped the pandemic uninfected. In particular, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, and Norfolk Island are supposed to have escaped due to an Australian policy of protective sequestration. In fact, archival accounts from local colonial officials, newspapers, and missionaries document how sequestration failed and severe influenza epidemics broke out across each of these territories in 1918–20. These “missing” epidemics challenge our understanding of the pandemic’s virulence, evolution, incubation period, and interaction with prior immunity, as well as how difficult it was to implement sequestration. These islands also reveal the global dispersion of the pandemic’s herald wave, and they help reveal the highly deadly wave of the pandemic that struck the Southern Hemisphere in mid-1921. We also document how early twentieth-century biomedical hubris and racist notions of Indigenous islanders’ health conspired to obscure the history of the pandemic in this region.

articles.title: Undisclosed Scaling: Reverse Engineering the Scoring Methodology of Mongolia's National Entrance Exam
articles.authors: Unubold Tuvshinjargal; Gan-Od Munkhtogtokh
articles.abstract: The Education Evaluation Center (EEC), which administers Mongolia's University Entrance Examination (ЭЕШ), states that raw examinee scores ``often approximate a normal distribution'' and describes its procedure for converting raw scores to the official 200--800 scaled score only as a transformation applied when this assumption fails, without disclosing the transformation itself. No prior study has tested this claim or identified the methodology actually in use. Using 260,319 individual-level student-subject records from the 2025 and 2026 administrations across all ten ЭЕШ subjects, we first test the normality assumption directly: raw-score distributions are rejected as normal in all twenty subject-year cohorts, with eighteen showing pronounced skewness, including the three highest-volume subjects that together account for the majority of examinees. We then reconstruct the actual scaling procedure by fitting five candidate models against the official scaled scores. A rank-based inverse-normal transformation reproduces the official mapping to rounding-level precision (MAE 0.2--0.4 points) in nineteen of twenty cohorts, applied uniformly regardless of distributional shape rather than conditionally as described. The sole exception, Russian 2026, instead follows an undisclosed linear formula that produced a roughly 69-point scaled-score advantage for that cohort relative to every other subject. We further show that the reporting scale's hard ceiling erases meaningful distinctions among top performers in exactly the cohorts where admissions competition is most intense. These findings demonstrate that a high-stakes national examination's actual scoring methodology can be reconstructed from public data alone, and that it materially diverges from the institution's own published account of it.

articles.title: “It’s Hard to See It Through Clinical Eyes When It’s Yourself”:    General Practice and Community Healthcare Professionals’ Experiences of Domestic Abuse, Disclosure, & Help-Seeking
articles.authors: Sandi Dheensa; Rebecca Cox; Judith Worthington; Paula Whittaker; Gene Feder; Alison Gregory
articles.abstract:
Background
Domestic abuse is highly prevalent and causes wide-ranging harms. Healthcare professionals are especially likely to receive disclosures and international policies call for a robust healthcare response to abuse.  But the needs of affected healthcare professionals (HCPs) have been sidelined. Globally, 42% of female HCPs report lifetime experience of domestic abuse. Our study aimed to explore how experiencing domestic abuse affects HCPs to understand the safety and support interventions needed. 
Methods
We used semi-structured interviews with 18 National Health Service primary and community HCPs and used Framework Analysis, drawing on four interrelated concepts: problem recognition, stigma, candidacy, and professional identity.  
Results
Perpetrators used HCP-survivors’ roles against them and domestic abuse had wide-ranging consequences for work. Remaining themes mapped onto HCP-survivors’ trajectory towards support, including problems with recognising and/or naming domestic abuse, the impact of recognising and naming it, reflections on different support options, consequences of workplace disclosure, support experiences, and reflections on what needs to change. Professional identity and profession-related factors affected each aspect of this trajectory, delaying recognition of domestic abuse and making help-seeking and positive support experiences less likely.  
Conclusion
Building an effective and compassionate healthcare response to domestic abuse will be impossible without attending to HCP-survivors’ needs and the inadequate responses of fellow HCPs. HCP-survivors are likely assets in improving responses to patients, colleagues, and students; but without support may experience trauma symptoms. We recommend improved first-line responses to HCP-survivors in workplaces and a move towards a recognition of HCPs as potential survivors in domestic abuse education, funding, and interventions.

articles.title: Do Population Transfers Weaken Partisan Uprisings? Postwar Poland's Operation Vistula
articles.authors: Anselm Hager; Krzysztof Krakowski
articles.abstract: Governments have long used population transfers to suppress partisan uprisings. By resettling outsiders into rebel strongholds, authorities seek to disrupt local networks and deprive insurgents of civilian support. We argue that such transfers can backfire, reinforcing partisan resolve. First, population transfers generate grievances that give incentives for cooperation between groups that would otherwise remain separate. Second, by reshuffling social ties, transfers force partisans to reinvest in trust-building exercises, creating a new organizational motive for renewed resistance. Exploiting Poland's post-World War II Operation Vistula as a natural experiment, we show that large-scale resettling of Ukrainians into partisan territories increased, rather than reduced, insurgent activity. In line with our mechanisms, we document the formation of enemy-of-the-enemy alliances between displaced populations and local partisans, and the intensification of coordination-building sabotage. We also show that, in the long term, transfer-exposed communities organized more anti-regime strikes during the 1980s Solidarność movement.

articles.title: Dynastic dynamics: Modelling powerful naming choices with stochastic prestige
articles.authors: Pablo Rosillo-Rodes; Santiago Lamata-Otín; David Soriano-Paños; Laurent Hébert-Dufresne; Peter Sheridan Dodds
articles.abstract: The naming choices of powerful rulers encode millennia of cultural, political, and institutional influences. Consequently, the long-term onomastic dynamics within some of the most powerful dynasties cannot be explained by simple mechanisms such as frequency-dependent reinforcement or random name reuse. Here, we propose a minimal model that encapsulates these influences in a single highly stochastic variable, prestige, and assume that name selection is driven by the prestige accumulated by previous rulers bearing the same name within each dynasty. Using an extensive dataset spanning ten dynasties, we show that the model reproduces the pronounced inequalities in name frequencies, the long-term persistence of dominant names, and the abrupt rises in popularity observed in historical records. Our results suggest that the naming traditions of powerful rulers preserve institutional memory through reinforcement while remaining sensitive to rare historical events that can reshape the hierarchy of names across generations.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Innovations and Election Administration in Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Babatunde A. Agbeyangi; Oluwatobi N. Ogunnusi; Abiodun B. Oluseye
